We've developed an explicit expression for the first order deformation of G2-instantons. Utilizing this expression, we were able to derive the abundance equation for abelian instantons. Our findings show that, in terms of deformation, abelian G2-instantons are fully rigid. We were also able to confirm a previous conjecture made by Donaldson and Sullivan. Furthermore, the expression for first order deformation allowed us to analyze the preservation of the abelian nature under deformation. Our research shows that the subalgebra of the adjoint action which preserves the abelian nature is commutative. We were able to translate the general deformation expression into a more practical form for practical applications.

To establish the normality of operators in specific Hilbert spaces, we initially need to identify when certain operators are normal. We focus on composition operators and weighted composition operators to determine their normality in particular spaces. Our analysis involves evaluating weighted composition operators and operators in space of analytic functions for p-values and also involves evaluating weighted composition operators on the space of meromorphic functions for p-values.

A detailed mathematical analysis of the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions of $N$ in terms of their parts and differences is presented. We demonstrate the $p$-periodicity in these intrinsic features and establish connections with the number of certain $p$-partitions of nodes in these partitions. Ultimately, formulas for the $p$-periods of the sequences are derived.

Three-dimensional point cloud models are gaining traction in real-world applications, but they face challenges due to the lack of robust methods for handling geometric distortifications. A new 3D point transformation framework has been developed that accounts for geometric distortifications and ensures reliable model performance. Through thorough testing, this framework outperforms existing methods for certifying accuracy against distortifications and enhances 3D model resilience by up to 20% while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Additionally, this framework is efficiently executable, requiring only 1.5 times more processing power than evaluating a standard 3D model.

This research introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing and assessing the reliability of Grouped Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (GFCW) and Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks. We develop a mathematical model that enables the calculation of interference probabilities, the frequency of collisions, and the efficiency of data transmission. We demonstrate the efficacy of grouping chirps into packets in enhancing system reliability and the practical feasibility of this approach. We analyze the impact of varying system parameters, such as the number of packets per data transmission and the distribution of data transmission timing, on performance metrics. We find that increasing the number of chirps per data transmission enhances interference probabilities but also boosts data transmission efficiency. We identify an optimal balance between these probabilities that maximizes efficiency, the transmission of data, and minimizes collisions. We also examine the effects of using unequal sweep durations and data transmission timing on performance, revealing that using a single sweep duration for all nodes and synchronized data transmission yields the most favorable outcomes.

Our study explores the detection of entangled two-photon absorption in non-linear materials using the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry technique. We've developed a theoretical framework to identify the visibility of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram as a definitive sign of entangled two-photon absorption. This framework considers the Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility as comprising a background component and an additional component influenced by the interaction between photons and the material. This understanding enables the separation of these two components through experiments involving both coherent and entangled photon pairs, thereby isolating the specific contribution of entangled two-photon absorption to the overall visibility. This approach has been applied to examine the entangled two-photon absorption properties of various materials, including tungsten trioxide and tungsten carbide, and our findings indicate that tungsten trioxide exhibits entangled two-photon absorption, while tungsten carbide exhibits bi-phhoton induced transparency.

Let $T$ be a one-dimensional torus and $X$ a complex, one-dimensional space that's equipped with $T$-action that's effective and algebraic in nature. The goal of this paper is to provide a solution to the classification of free actions of $T$-elliptic Hopf algebras that are related to $ell_\omega(X,\lambda)$ in the context of $ell_\omega(X,\lambda)$-affine spaces. The solution builds on a solution found by D. Gepner and M. Stolz for the case of action without any constraints.

This research addresses the problem of predicting missing connections in dynamic knowledge bases by incorporating time-based information. A novel method for representing time is proposed, incorporating cyclic patterns and drawing from existing ordinal and continuous time-scales. This representation enables the use of cyclic time features as additional, predictive attributes. To enhance the model's ability to capture evolving knowledge, we employ Poisson processes to model the frequency of knowledge base changes and incorporate this into our time-encoding scheme, which has been shown to outperform current state-of-the-art techniques on multiple datasets.

In this study, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the sound generated upon impact with various surfaces, including glass, wood, concrete, and metal surfaces. We found that the sound produced by the deformation of the ground is not only present but also the dominant component of the sound emitted, especially at low frequencies. This phenomenon is observable up to a distance of 10 meters and at frequencies below 100 Hz. We also discovered that the sound resulting from the impact's body sound propagation through the ground can be heard above the ambient ambient noise level in specific circumstances, such as when the impact's point of proximity to the sound measuring device is minimal. We developed an approach to distinguish between the sound generated by the impact's propagation through the air and the sound that travels through the ground, and with this approach, we were able to conclude that all types of impacts produce audible ground sound.

Quantum mechanics allows for idealized processes, but real-world applications often deviate from these ideals. Our research explores the implications of imperfect correlations in Bell nonlocal theories and technologies within the context of quantum information. We found that even slight imperfections in measurements can cause significant changes in nonlocal theories, whereas other aspects like the number of possible measurements remain largely unaffected. Our findings are based on theoretical models of imperfect honest parties and may have relevance to the study of Bell nonlocal correlations in technologies involving quantum mechanics.

Quasi-crystals, characterized by their non-periodic yet ordered structure, have been found in various forms, including metallic alloys and a specific type of two-dimensional tiling pattern known as the Kagome lattice. In an effort to understand the origins of this structure, researchers have been studying a two-dimensional Kagome quasicrystal derived from a specific mathematical representation of the lattice, resulting in an infinite, highly symmetric structure. In contrast to conventional materials, these studies have revealed that introducing randomness does not eliminate the structure's inherent flat energy bands, an phenomenon that can be attributed to the structure's inherent symmetry. Furthermore, researchers have found that this phenomenon persists even when the structure is not fully symmetric, as long as specific symmetries within it are maintained. In addition to its significance in two-dimensional materials, this phenomenon has been found to manifest in higher-dimensional systems, an observation that has implications for understanding the behavior of topological materials.

In recent years, research on two-dimensional materials has gained significant momentum due to the exceptional properties of graphene. The discovery of numerous new 2D materials, particularly within the TMD family, has led to the emergence of numerous theoretical predictions. A particular type of material, hydrogen boride monolayers with trigonal lattice structure, has been of particular interest due to its unique properties. However, its stability in ambient conditions remains uncertain. To address this, a theoretical investigation was conducted to analyze the electronic and phonon properties of this material. The results indicate that hydrogen plays a significant role in enhancing electron-phonon interactions, thereby increasing its potential stability. The analysis also reveals that hydrogen boride monolayers with trigonal lattice structure exhibits superconducting behavior, with a critical temperature exceeding 10K.

In 1999, Gouyou-Beauchamps established a connection between key values of Kreweras' flattened partition numbers through decreased runs, and this relationship is now extended to variants of these values as $f_{n, k}$, for which a novel proof is provided using generating functions.

A key difference between the behavior of ergodic dynamical systems derived from actions of finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups and those of toroidal nature lies in the existence, in the former but not the latter, of a non-constant continuous function on the space of characters that remains invariant under the group action's action on characters. A new class of discrete, geometrically ergodic groups has been identified that do not admit an invariant measure, yet can be represented as subgroups of finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups do admit such a function.

Automotive companies are increasingly adopting formal verification methods, like model checking, to validate automotive active safety systems. To address the complex nature of modern automotive systems, which often involve continuous variables and infinite state spaces, researchers have developed various approaches to handle model checking with a focus on safety and functional correctness. This paper provides an in-depth review of recent advancements in model checking for automotive active safety systems, discussing the benefits and limitations of different methods and highlighting open issues that need to be addressed in the future.

System identification of complex nonlinear systems in a general setting using the Koopman operator is considered in this study. Under certain conditions, it is demonstrated that nonlinear scalar autoregressive models with noise can have noise-free expansions that converge uniformly to the system's true evolution, and these models are shown to be effectively approximated by linear models. It is further proven that Koopman operator-based models selected through standard model selection techniques will converge to a unique, consistent result as measurement errors decrease and data sampling becomes充分 as measurement errors decrease and data sampling becomes充分.

Investigating the origins of Leibniz's concepts of bounded and unbounded infinity, we uncover that bounded infinity corresponds to potential infinity, while unbounded infinity corresponds to actual infinity. We demonstrate that these conceptions of infinity can be traced back to early Church Fathers and were also present in Aristotle's work, despite his rejection of unbounded actual infinities. It is also noted that these conceptions of bounded and unbounded infinity can be found in the mathematical work of Georg Cantor.

The Planck satellite's 2013 data release included full sky maps of the cosmic microwave background temperature and polarization, generated after eliminating the effects of foreground interference. This removal process involved subtracting estimates of foreground noise, which can introduce inaccuracies in the data that may impact scientific research. This study investigates how foreground removal impacts temperature and polarization parameter estimation using simulations based on the Planck satellite's data analysis. These simulations show that foreground removal can introduce significant biases in certain parameters, particularly planckium, which is sensitive to noise in the data, and foreground removal can have a substantial impact on its estimation. These findings suggest that future space-based missions should consider the potential effects of foreground interference when analyzing their data.

The paper examines operators that maintain or reduce the linear independence of vector sequences, specifically examining the mappings of vector sequences in Hilbert space into closed subspaces and into spaces of square-integrable functions of a unit vector, with an emphasis on preserving the l0-norm of vector sequences, i.e., the number of non-zero elements, in both closed subspaces and function spaces of square-integrable functions of a unit vector, providing relevant examples and counterexamples, as well as essential theorems and lemmas, specifically involving projections of orthogonal bases and l0-norm preservation, and the representations of linear operators based on their actions on a specific set of vector sequences, and the solutions to related extremum problems,

Document modeling-based methods in recommender systems have shown significant potential in enhancing recommendation accuracy and personalization.  However, their effectiveness is hindered due to their reliance on document metadata and item profiles, which are often incomplete or inaccurate.  To address this limitation, our study focuses on improving the representation of documents and items by incorporating text-based information.  To achieve this, we propose a novel text-based recommendation framework called RecText, which integrates a natural language processing model to capture the semantic relationships between text snippets and recommendations.  Our experiments demonstrate that RecText outperforms current state-of-the-art document modeling-based methods and provides better personalization by leveraging text information.

Building on previous work by Bordenave and Chayes, this study extends their findings to a broader class of ensembles of delocalized unitary matrices. Specifically, it proves that when two such matrices are randomly combined, their interaction behaves as if it's independently and freely random, provided each individual matrix is also freely random on its own. This important conclusion has practical implications for the field of random matrix theory, particularly in demonstrating that certain randomly constructed matrices satisfy the conditions of delocalization and having isolated eigenvalues, without requiring strict structural constraints.

In real-time systems with uncertain timing, monitoring strategies need to be flexible and adaptable.  To be effective, these monitoring strategies should be able to account for timing uncertainty, which in turn requires the creation of timing-aware monitoring tools.  To meet this requirement, we have developed a monitoring system that can handle the 3C model of timing, allowing it to create timing-aware monitoring tools.  To achieve this, the system uses statistical methods to determine the upper limits of monitoring thresholds, which are then used to create monitors that can tolerate a specified level of timing uncertainty.  To make the system more efficient, we have designed these monitors to be lightweight and easy to implement, allowing it to be used in a wide range of systems and environments.

A search for the $J/\psi$ resonance $a_0(980)$ and an investigation into its potential connection to the $J/\psi p \bar{p}$ interaction at low energies have been conducted using data collected by the BESIII experiment at centers operating at different energy levels, totaling 2.63 petabytes of data. The experiment identified the $a_0(980)$ resonance, and the research yielded a maximum likelihood estimate for the branching fraction of the $J/\psi$ decay into the $f_0(980)$ and proton-antiproton particles, resulting in a fraction of approximately 0.0041 with the associated error margin of 0.0019. The findings also showed that the relative phase between the coupled decay channels decays $J/\psi \to a_0(980) \to \gamma \pi^0 \pi^0$ and $J/\psi \to a_0(980) \to f_0(980) \to \pi^+ \pi^-$ is approximately 180°, with the margin of error at 22°. The research further explored the implications of these findings on the $a_0(980)$ interaction with the $J/\psi$ particle and the strong interaction of the proton and antiproton, concluding that the $a_0(980)$

The fourth-generation Very Large Telescope Interferometer's core component, the GRAVITY camera, has enabled groundbreaking astronomical discoveries thanks to its exceptional precision and sensitivity. To maintain optimal performance, real-time adjustments are made to the connected telescopes based on data collected by the camera. These adjustments, known as stabilizations, are carried out using four dedicated devices called acquisition cameras, which monitor the light from the science camera's image. The data gathered from these devices have been found to refine the algorithm governing the telescopes' adjustments, resulting in even more precise data. This research outlines the process of training the algorithm that analyzes data from the acquisition cameras and demonstrates its ability to replace the existing acquisition cameras, resulting in minimal lag and improved operational efficiency.

We investigate the approximability of the Capacitated k-Center (CkC) and the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) problems within the class of graphs characterized by a specific dimension. In an effort to overcome a barrier to polynomial-time approximation introduced by Levy et al. (FOCS 2019), we introduce a new dimension measure and provide an 8-approximation algorithm for CkSwO on graphs with this dimension, leading to a constant-factor approximation in cases where the dimension is polynomially bounded. This result stands in contrast to the observed difficulty in achieving similar approximation for CkC on the same type of graphs, with the primary distinction being that CkSwO allows for excluded vertices, a factor that enables its solution to be based on a more efficient clustering approach.

In the case of entire functions where the hyper order is less than 1/2, the third author of this study proved that the Brück conjecture holds, assuming the value of the coefficient alpha is not -1. This study aims to extend the result to meromorphic functions with a deficiency value of -1 for the value 0, provided the L-exceptional value alpha is not -1 or a negative integer less than -L.

This research presents an updated version of the initial algorithm outlined in a previous paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06002). The original algorithm was designed to determine a low-rank polynomial matrix over a finite field, given a set of potentially inaccurate entries. The revised algorithm significantly reduced its evaluation count when dealing with clean data sets, yet it still struggled in the presence of errors. We have now redesigned a set of optimizations that significantly decreased its engine's evaluation count even in the most challenging scenarios.

In this research, we present a novel technique for controlling the simultaneous emission of paired and odd-correlated photons from Cavity QED systems interacting with two-photon and single-photon Cavity QED systems. The operator characteristics of the Cavity QED operator enable the transition between the emission of paired and odd-correlated photons. The proposed method offers an improved approach to on-demand generation of paired and odd-correlated photon states, which may have applications in quantum communication and computing.

Using ab initio calculations, we've investigated the principle of corresponding states at high pressures, comparing it across different alkali elements. We've computed the equation of state, interstitial electronic structures, zero-temperature Gr\"uneisen constants, and ionization potentials. The results show that the principle of corresponding states applies to alkali elements, as evidenced by the equation of state following a universal trend when plotted on a specific scale, and the elements exhibiting similar electronic structures at corresponding positions.

In a medium that breaks parity locally, the masses and interaction potentials of vector mesons are altered, allowing for an expanded understanding of their properties. Our research involves a vector meson theory with local parity breaking, resulting in the Chern-Simons term appearing in the vector meson's effective action in 3D space. The appearance of the Chern-Simons term causes the vector mesons to acquire properties similar to anyonic particles, with their helicities being a a function of momentum. Additionally, the Chern-Simons term induces an interaction between the longitudinal component of one vector meson and the transverse components of another vector meson, as well as a scalar particle. This gives rise to an interaction potential exhibiting an asymmetric Yuki potential characteristic. The Yuki potential's minimum can be adjusted by varying the parity breaking order parameter and the Chern-Simons coupling. The research has implications for the study of vector meson production and scattering, particularly in the context of the direct photon to vector meson conversion process observed in heavy ion collisions.

A distributed size estimation network algorithm is proposed, which can be implemented in both directed and undirected networks. The method relies on nodes selecting random network paths and transmitting identifiers to the network's exit node, which then calculates the network size based on the received data. To counter potential issues with malicious nodes that could distort the results, a distributed algorithm is designed and analyzed, which can adapt to changes in other nodes' selection parameters and account for potential malicious interference. The performance of this algorithm is tested through simulation and demonstrates its resilience in networks containing 10% malicious nodes.

A novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in asymptotically flat initial data sets with compact support is presented. Unlike conventional methods, this scheme doesn't seek a fully regular solution for the conformal factor, rather it targets a solution that remains zero outside a specific bounded region and remains smooth within that region. By defining a solution to the Laplace equation within a region and continuously extending it to zero outside, the method ensures the new Hamiltonian constraint is satisfied. Furthermore, this scheme can be adapted for use in region-based numerical methods.

The main detectors in the JUNO experiment, consisting of 20,000 ton of liquid scintillator, are designed to identify particles based on their interaction-induced photons, which are detected using 0.1% pure photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) with high-sensitivity to visible light. These detectors are planned to be housed in an underground facility at the site in Dongguan, Guangdong, China, and are anticipated to discover the standard model neutrino mass hierarchy by analyzing the nearby reactor antineutrinos, along with other particles, including dark matter, neutrinos, and specific short-lived mesons, with the latter two being detected using the 2.5 km$^2$-water Cherenkov detectors, which are designed to detect distant sources, such as supernovae, neutrinos from the Earth's core, and high-energy neutrinos, with the detectors' primary goal of discovering new physics beyond the standard model.

The Informer model introduced structure-aware attention to reduce self-attention
complexity to O(log N), but it was found to struggle with capturing dimensional
relationships in multidimensional time series tasks. To overcome this limitation, 
we propose enhanced versions of the Informer model for both single-value and multi-value 
predictions. By adding a dimension aggregation module and using a knowledge
distillation approach, our models can learn and capture dimensional relationships
better, resulting in improved overall performance. Experiments on real-world datasets
confirm the effectiveness of our models in outperforming existing methods.

To assess the performance of different ADC designs, we examine their sensitivity to variations in the atmosphere using metrics like the RMS error and Admittance. Our study compares two widely used models, the ADC and MOD09, with the latter exhibiting a more pronounced error in simulating blue range spectra, rendering it less suitable for our purposes.

Ensemble methods, long established in machine learning, have seen a recent resurgence in the context of large language models (LLMs). A notable approach, logits ensemble, enhances performance by merging the outputs of multiple models. Building on this, we introduce PILE, a method that incorporates a tree-based structure and utilizes captions to optimize an initial model selection process, as well as to refine an output explanation. PILE's capabilities do not rely on any modifications to the base models, nor does it demand additional computational resources, making it an effective method for leveraging existing models. Our experiments on various datasets, including GSM8K, demonstrate PILE's superior performance compared to existing ensemble approaches, and PILE's simplicity and lack of requirement for modified base models or extra computation make it an effective method for leveraging existing models.

We investigate a network of sensors to detect ultra-light bosonic dark matter-induced stochastic intensity fluctuations. Our research focuses on the optimal configuration of sensor networks to maximize detection efficiency. By analyzing individual sensor data and cross-correlations between sensor pairs, we can enhance our ability to distinguish signal from background noise. Network optimization is crucial, particularly when considering the placement of sensors in diverse environments to minimize redundant information and maximize overall detection sensitivity.

We examine the efficiency of the basis pursuit method in finding exact, exact-order sparse solutions for underdetermined linear systems, particularly focusing on the role of system matrix properties and additional information. The problem's ease of recovery is influenced by the basis pursuit candidate set, and we analyze this in the context of systems with a specific matrix spectrum and an orthogonal or incoherent basis. Additionally, we explore the effect of having access to a linear combination of the solution, and we consider its impact when the system matrix has a compressed sensing structure.

A novel approach to supercomputing, based on programmable switches, has gained significant attention recently. However, a significant challenge in this domain is the scarcity of open-source compiler backends for emerging architectures, resulting in an incomplete software stack. To bridge this gap, we have developed an open-source compiler backend for P4.1/P4.2 programs running on PTF4 programmable processors, and have made it available for an existing SuperMUC-NG supercomputer equipped with PTF4 processors. Our developed backend is highly functional and efficient, enabling the execution of a wide range of programs, including a DNS resolver, network flow monitoring, a network-based Pong application, P2P protocols, and a network load testing protocol. Our extensive testing has validated the correctness and performance of our developed backend, and our code is now publicly accessible on GitHub.

A common approach to solving the vector transport equation is to use the weak form of the equation with the upwind scheme to ensure stability. In this research, we develop an efficient and accurate method to solve the vector transport equation by using a mixed finite element formulation. This approach utilizes the exact divergence of basis functions to ensure local mass conservation, resulting in improved overall mass error and more accurate phase average errors. By formulating the equation in its strong form and discretizing it with first-order linear elements in the cross-stream direction and a stable upwind scheme along streamlines, we demonstrate significant reductions in both error metrics compared to traditional methods that use standard streamline upwind Petrov-Galerkin (SUPG) forms.

Machine learning advancements are increasingly accompanied by a need to address ethical considerations.  To address this need, research in areas such as privacy, security, and robustness is growing in importance.  Specifically, research in federated learning, differential privacy, and fairness metrics is gaining momentum in response to these advancements.  This article provides an in-depth examination of these three areas, along with other related concepts, in addressing the ethical challenges of machine learning.  It also outlines key research directions for the future and discusses the potential benefits of combining these three areas in addressing ethical concerns.

Recent data from the LHCb experiment, specifically from their Detached Charm production run, provided evidence for two excited states of the $B_c^+$ particle. Analysis of the $B_c^+ B_\overline c$ system's mass spectrum revealed the existence of these states, designated as $B_c(3095)^+$ and $B_c(3132)^+$. These states correspond to different rotational and vibrational energy levels and align with theoretical predictions.

Researchers have been exploring continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods, which can be seen as a combination of classic Runge-Kutta methods in multiple dimensions and finite-Butcher array Runge-Kutta methods. These methods have been developed to address specific problems, including Hamiltonian systems, systems with conservation properties, and differential-algebraic equations. A new way of creating butcher-floquet diagrams for continuous-stage methods, which are useful in analyzing their properties, has been found to have applications beyond just the solution of ordinary differential equations, including finite-element discretizations of problems, like the Keller-Segel model, and even in the study of the Riemann-Hilbert problem.

This research explores a novel technique for optimizing the training of neural networks, including various architectures like convolutional and recurrent neural networks, by utilizing data-independent gradients. A specific application of this technique involves training image classifiers using Game Theory's minimax approach, where a primary model and a secondary critic network are trained to compete with each other. By having the critic network process a reduced number of training samples in parallel, the primary model achieves training speeds comparable to GANs while maintaining higher accuracy.

In the study of boundary value problems associated with chaotic systems, it is essential to understand how energy loss influences the system's behavior. To achieve this, researchers have developed methods to calculate how small energy loss affects two key properties of the system: the stability of different areas the system can occupy and the average time it takes for particles to traverse different regions of the phase space. The methods involve using two different techniques, one based on linearizing the system and the other using a special statistical distribution, to determine how small energy loss influences these properties. The methods have been successfully applied to two examples, the scattering of particles in a set of interconnected areas and the movement of a particle in a confined space, to understand how energy loss influences different aspects of the system's behavior.

The muon g-2 collaboration recently announced that their new measurement of the muon's magnetic moment anomaly aligns with the anomaly's expected value based on particle physics theories. However, the measured anomaly does not align with the predictions made by the Standard Model. A potential explanation for this anomaly could be the existence of new physics involving light particles known as axion-like particles. These particles might be created through a process involving the conversion of two photons into these particles. Future experiments at the Jefferson Lab's Electron Ion Collider and the Brookhaven National Laboratory's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider will be able to explore the parameter space of these particles more comprehensively and at a much higher rate than current experiments.

This study introduces a novel video action recognition framework, the Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), which effectively integrates global and local features to enhance action recognition performance. The core of HAN is its innovative multiple-step spatial-temporal attention mechanism, which identifies key areas within spatial-temporal feature maps and assigns corresponding weights. During the first step, HAN highlights action-related regions by filtering out background interference, then in the second step, it pinpoints sub-region importance and localizes specific key areas and joint positions. The generated attention maps then guide HAN to focus on the most informative action regions. Moreover, HAN's memory-based recurrent structure enables it to progressively incorporate information from subsequent joint detection steps. Additionally, HAN is capable of combining backbone features and hand-crafted AMIK features through a hybrid fusion module, thereby achieving superior performance. Notably, HAN attains impressive state-of-the-art results on the KITTI dataset, with a 70.4% top-1 accuracy rate at a 25-frame offset, outperforming existing methods by 3.4 percentage points.

Our research involves analyzing how black holes with very high spin rates behave when hit by scattered particles in the presence of intense gravitational forces. We examined two distinct scenarios: one where the black hole is almost at its maximum spin capacity, and another where it is at its maximum spin capacity. In both cases, we found that the black hole's future state depends heavily on its initial state. When the black hole is almost at its maximum spin capacity, it splits into two parts, with each part having its own separate event horizon. On the other hand, when the black hole is at its maximum spin capacity, it splits into two parts, with one part having its maximum spin capacity, and the other part having a lower spin capacity, with its event horizon extending to infinity. Additionally, we found that when near-spinning black holes merge, the resulting spin rate of the new black hole is always lower than the sum of the spin rates of the original black holes.

The emergence of life in the cosmos is a pressing inquiry in astronomy, with a significant connection to star formation. As star-forming regions serve as the primary source of heavy elements essential for life, they are a primary focus of astronomical research. Star-forming regions also house cosmic dust particles, which are thought to act as catalysts for the creation of complex molecules, including those vital for the development of life. Furthermore, they are home to cosmic magnetic fields, which are thought to be a prerequisite for the existence of life. By studying the star-forming region, astronomers can gain a deeper understanding of the cosmic environment in which life may have originated.

The calculation of entropy for complex probability distributions often proves infeasible due to the lack of direct evaluation methods. A new approach has been developed to overcome this limitation by adapting a traditional formula for entropy calculation. This formula, which involves infinite series, can be utilized to compute entropy for probability distributions that cannot be directly evaluated. However, this approach has certain drawbacks, such as slow convergence and the need for special functions, which can limit its applicability. To overcome these limitations, an alternative method for calculating entropy has been developed. This method relies on a fundamental property of the logarithm function and uses finite sums to calculate entropy, making it applicable to a wide range of probability distributions. This new approach has been successfully applied to calculate the entropy of the generalized normal distribution, for which no closed-form solution previously existed.

Modeling of discrete event systems relies on boron measures and markov processes in semiconductors. A model of a semiconductor manufacturing system is developed using Borel measures on state and flux spaces, along with a Markov process that determines state and flux transitions. Analyzing such a model is complicated, so a model reduction method is applied, which is also applicable to other measures-based models. A method of state and flux aggregation in Borel measures-based discrete event systems is introduced, which is then used to simplify the manufacturing system model through a three-stage process. A resulting aggregated model, consisting of countable state and finite Borel measures on flux space, is obtained, but it still poses analytical challenges. To address this, a further method of countable state aggregation is applied, leading to a countable state and finite flux aggregated model.

Network security is increasingly reliant on machine learning, yet a significant hurdle remains in deploying resource-intensive classifiers on devices with limited resources. The proposed solution, NBcoded, overcomes this challenge by translating complex neural network models into efficient Naive Bayes algorithms without compromising their classification accuracy. The model transformation process involves extracting key features and parameters from the original neural network, which are then used to generate an equivalent Bayes classifier. When evaluated on a large dataset of malicious applications, NBcoded demonstrated comparable accuracy to the original neural network models. The resulting algorithm is not only easier to implement but also requires less processing power and analysis time compared to the initial classifiers.

For the class of metabelian groups, we establish an upper limit on the growth rate disparity within each subgroup and subgroup of finite index. Furthermore, we obtain a tighter constraint when considering only those metabelian groups that are both finitely presented and torsion-free. Our research also provides examples of metabelian groups where the achieved growth rate disparity is at its maximum.

A new approach has been developed to differentiate between the trajectories of living entities and non-biological objects. The method relies on extracting distinctive features from trajectory data and using a machine learning classifier. We've tested this approach with synthetic trajectories based on different motion models, as well as real trajectory datasets of bacteria influenced by external factors and the movements of pedestrians in a city center. A novel method combining quantum and classical techniques is proposed for solving
complex optimization issues in power networks, specifically addressing the challenge
of power system partitioning. The algorithm, developed using the QUBO framework and
D-Wave quantum annealing machine, incorporates a classical simulated退火 algorithm
for refinement. Experimental results using the D-Wave 2000Q machine demonstrate
that the hybrid and purely classical methods yield partitioning solutions of
comparable quality, but the hybrid approach runs significantly faster,
particularly as the size of the test cases increases.

This study develops a probabilistic model to analyze the falling process of an object in a complex environment, taking into account two key factors: unsteady fluid drag forces and noise from digital measurements. We utilize a state estimator to track the object's state while distinguishing between the noise of measurements and the unsteady forces. By combining a fundamental physics model with a Bayesian approach, we create a Bayesian physics network that can be trained to differentiate between two forces and accurately identify the unsteady force causing the drag. This study presents a novel method for analyzing a specific unsteady force and provides a framework for further exploration of similar forces in a wide range of applications.

We investigate the LHC's capacity to detect the scenario where supersymmetry is realized through a hidden sector that interacts with the rest of the universe via a portal to the Z-higgs portal. This scenario is characterized by the presence of long-lived, colorless particles that are produced in pairs and then decay into a pair of electrically neutral, long-lived particles with a mass range of 100 GeV to 3 TeV. These particles decay into a pair of stable, long-lived particles that leave distinct signatures in the LHC's detectors. Our analysis focuses on the production and detection of these particles in the full 13 TeV LHC dataset, taking into account their colorless nature and the challenges in identifying them.

A key challenge in developing on-chip single-photon sources is the difficulty of collecting the emitted photons. To overcome this issue, we propose a design featuring a multi-quantum dot system aligned along the axis of a waveguide. By incorporating a specific taper section within the waveguide, we significantly enhance the collection efficiency of the emitted photons. The use of a short intrinsic active region reduces self-interaction between the dots and allows for a high density of optical modes due to the low mode volume created by the waveguide's high-quality factor and small effective mode area in the tapered area. Theoretical analysis indicates that our multi-QD system can achieve a high efficiency of around 80% and an extremely fast repetition rate of approximately 100 MHz.

The research examines how longitudinal sound waves are damped in a disordered material at low frequencies and low temperatures, with the findings showing that the damping follows a specific pattern, described by a power law at low frequencies and temperature, and transitions to a different power law at higher frequencies and temperatures. The study reveals that the power in the initial pattern is related to the spatial characteristics of the material's potential wells, specifically stating that the exponent in the pattern corresponds to the fractal dimension of these structures minus two. The results also showing that the pattern becomes similar to what is seen in regular three-dimensional scenarios when the fractal dimension reaches four, with these characteristics becoming more pronounced as the material's disorder increases.

We introduce a novel method for combining numerical and analytical techniques to calculate particles with complex relationships, enhancing the precision of numerical results while maintaining simplicity of numerical expressions. This method is applied to the 2-loop mass calculations of neutral BSM bosons within the context of the $s$-channel process $ZZH$. The computed results are then compared to results from the public code FanSahm, demonstrating the developed approach's high precision and efficiency.

We've developed a theoretical framework to examine how intense light interacts with complex systems of randomly distributed particles. This system's total light intensity can be broken down into distinct patterns, each associated with a specific frequency. Using the principles of frequency coherence and temporal fluctuations, we can describe each pattern as dependent on independent variables. This has led to a classification of systems into two types based on their interaction with light: those that follow classical laws and those that break these laws. This framework has been experimentally tested with a water-based system containing tiny particles, with a particular focus on light that exists in multiple intense forms simultaneously. This has been made possible with the development of a new light source that can create multiple, independent forms of intense light at the same time.

Recent observations from the Gaia Data Release 3 have provided significant evidence for a bar at the center of our galaxy. This bar is characterized by high non-axisymmetric radial velocity patterns and an estimated rotation speed of around 30-40 km/s. Based on these findings, researchers developed models to determine the bar's orientation, shape, and tilt relative to the galaxy's midplane. These models suggest that the bar is rotated approximately 20-30 degrees from the galaxy's midplane. Additionally, analysis of the bar's pattern speed indicates that it slowed down over time, similar to the process described by the fission instability theory.

Multi-modal optimization seeks a diverse range of optimal solutions while multi-objective optimization aims to discover various objectives' compromise solutions. Although both optimizations produce multiple optima, the former focuses on achieving a single, robust solution with high performance, while the latter prioritizes finding objectives-solutions that perform well collectively. As multi-modal optimization often yields superior results, it has gained significant interest in solving complex problems. However, a lack of clear definition and evaluation metrics hinders its practical application. This study proposes a multi-modal optimization framework that incorporates both single-objective and evolutionary algorithms. A comprehensive analysis of various approaches is presented, and a novel method utilizing a Gaussian process and adaptive sampling technique is developed to efficiently explore the fitness-landscape. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of solution diversity and quality, as demonstrated by extensive experiments.

Our research focuses on the stable matching problem in a many-to-one setting with an even number of participants. We investigate the partitional stable matching problem, in which matchings are divided into two categories: those that also maximize welfare, and those that maintain stability while producing a wide range of welfare outcomes. We establish the computational boundaries for these categories when the utility functions of the agents are related and have a binary valuation system. Our analysis reveals that while related binary functions make the problem tractable in many-to-one settings, its tractability in many-to-many settings remains an unresolved issue. Additionally, the case of arbitrary binary functions in many-to-one settings is also a subject of ongoing investigation.

In a system under strain, the valley Hall effect is significantly impacted.
The effect of non-uniform strain, however, remains unclear.
To investigate this, we studied a system where both valley Hall currents and strain are present.
Our research reveals that under random strain conditions, there is an optimal level of strain that maximizes valley Hall currents.
Additionally, we found that gradients in strain not only impede valley Hall currents but also cause them to exhibit a preferred direction based on the orientation of the strain.

We extend the concept of stabilizers for equidistant sets within metric spaces, leading to the definition of stabilizers for stabilizer networks, which we refer to as stabilizers of networks, and further explore the properties of these stabilizers, including the existence of a central point for clouds with non-trivial stabilizers, and relationships between the size of these central points and the network's stabilizer size, as well as connections between the stabilizer sizes of related network types, and this investigation also reveals insights into the geometry of stabilizer groups for these networks, which often possess an abelian structure, before finally drawing a parallel between our findings and the research on network curvature, showing that certain properties of networks with high curvature are analogous to the properties of networks with large stabilizers.

A dual circularly polarized patch antenna with dual feed lines is designed to support GPS and GLONASS frequencies. The antenna features two orthogonal modes that are excited in equal magnitude and phase to achieve circular polarization. With two 50-ohm microstrip feed lines placed at the center and edge of the radiating patch, the antenna is designed to be compact and efficient. When implemented on a 0.127 cm thick substrate with a 101.6 cm x 101.6 cm ground plane, the antenna demonstrates excellent performance, with a 7 dBic isolation between the modes, a 3 to 7 dBi gain range, and a 10 to 15 degree half power beamwidth within a 1.57 GHz to 1.6135 GHz matched bandwidth.

Quantum error correction is crucial for building large-scale quantum computers, but current quantum processors have high error rates that overwhelm existing decoding methods. Therefore, there's a need for more efficient decoding techniques. Reinforcement learning has been applied to various error correction problems, but its potential in scattering-type near-field optical microscopy is yet to be explored. This study applies reinforcement learning to develop a more accurate detector in near-field optical microscopy, resulting in improved image quality and efficiency.

The measurements were taken in various momentum ranges and yield patterns were observed. The research found that as the momentum of the quarks decreases, the yield of the particles increases significantly. The increased yield is significantly higher than what would be expected from non-interacting particles. The increased yield is consistent with the idea that the particles interact with each other in a way that maximizes the effect. In this research, our group demonstrates the simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model using a trapped-ion system with a type of interaction called Ising interaction. By combining this with carefully designed single-qubit operations, we can produce effective coupling between adjacent qubits that can be adjusted over time to implement a type of interaction known as adiabatic. To overcome challenges related to simulating the Fermi-Hubbard model, we developed a method to introduce controlled noise through a type of interaction known as Zeeman, which helps to distinguish between different quantum states. A novel unsupervised learning algorithm called Bonsai is proposed to create adaptive feature sets that optimize downstream machine learning models. By adaptively selecting features and creating subspaces that enhance model performance, Bonsai is capable of operating with minimal or no labeled data. The algorithm's flexibility is further demonstrated through its ability to produce aggregate feature representations that can be utilized by multiple models simultaneously. The paper outlines two implementations of Bonsai - an offline method for feature selection and an online technique for real-time feature representation adaptation. The efficacy of Bonsai is substantiated through its superior performance in various applications, including voice activity detection, self-driving car development, and adaptive feature learning for multiple models.

A scattering medium, such as turbulent air or water, distorts light signals, making distant objects difficult to see. Researchers have developed an innovative approach using a weighted-mutation assisted genetic algorithm to restore the clarity of such distorted light. By combining this method with advanced computational techniques, they successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in a real-world experiment. They used the algorithm to reverse the effects of a 1 cm thick layer of milk suspended in water, and were able to clearly read a hidden symbol despite significant turbulence. Furthermore, they achieved a breakthrough by making the algorithm read two separate characters simultaneously, proving its high capacity for multi-channel data transmission.

Off-policy learning methods often rely on offline datasets to learn effective policies, but existing algorithms often produce poor value function estimates, leading to suboptimal policies. To address this issue, we propose a two-part solution, consisting of a testing-time augmentation method and a new algorithm for offline policy learning. Firstly, we develop a technique to generate more accurate value function estimates by leveraging multiple off-policy datasets, which can be used to correct over-optimistic estimates and improve the quality of policies learned. Secondly, we develop a new algorithm, called TTAAL, which utilizes these estimates to learn effective policies, and we demonstrate through experiments that it outperforms existing methods in a range of real-world scenarios.

The performance of collection methods in monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors was investigated by altering the sensor material. The thickness of the sensor layer was kept constant at around 5-7 micrometers, and the charge collection efficiency was measured using a 55Fe source. The charge collection capabilities were compared between two sensor materials: CGCO4 and CGCO6, and the results indicated that CGCO6 had better performance. The charge collection efficiency was also affected by the size of the collection area, with larger areas showing better efficiency. The relationship between collection area and charge collection efficiency was found to be consistent with simulation data.

A new generation of space-based telescopes is set to revolutionize our understanding of the universe, particularly with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which will provide unprecedented views of distant celestial objects. To complement this, a network of ground-based 30-meter class telescopes is being developed to enhance our planetary detection capabilities. We propose an innovative approach to streamline the data processing of these large-scale observatories by employing deep learning-based image analysis. Our method involves using convolutional neural networks to effectively utilize supercomputers for real-time data processing. Building on the success of the PlanetFinder algorithm in planet detection, we have created an open-source, Python-based image processing system that utilizes the latest deep learning techniques. Our approach balances detection sensitivity and computational efficiency by utilizing transfer learning and data augmentation. Our results demonstrate that this system can achieve a high detection rate for planets across a wide range of scenarios, ultimately allowing astronomers to focus on the most promising candidates for further analysis.

This study introduces a novel macro-finance model that can handle diverse and negative short-term interest rates. The model, which is consistent with no-arbitrage principles, incorporates the Arbitrage Pricing Theory (APT) in the form of factor models for rate dynamics. It is further enhanced by a statistical model that uses the multivariate skew-t distribution to predict the first-order factors, which are then treated as signals for a Kalman filter to track the first-order latent factors in Kalman-median form. Calibration to US short-term rate data from 1960 to 2019 shows that the model, which is both linear and non-Gaussian, effectively explains a significant portion of the variation in long-term Treasury yields and is supported by out-of-sample analysis of bond price variations.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment's (DUNE) data collection system, consisting of two parts - a 400-ton Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber at the Brookhaven National Laboratory test beam and a massive 40-kton chamber at the Sanford Underground Research Facility - will enable a comprehensive search for neutrino oscillations. Given that the DUNE's off-axis beam is primarily designed for neutrino mass research, its sensitivity to sterile neutrinos may be limited. However, the use of a specialized near-detector will expand this search domain. In this study, we outline the development of a dedicated simulation framework for neutrino models involving a fourth neutrino type, and we present initial findings on the DUNE's potential to detect sterile neutrinos through a near-detector utilizing three-dimensional reconstruction capabilities.

Paired data analysis is commonly used in various fields, including clinical trials, but often faces the issue of small sample sizes and limited degrees of freedom. In such cases, traditional estimators based on normal approximations are not reliable. In this research, we address this challenge by developing more accurate methods for making inferences within the general linear paired data framework. Our new approach involves creating fully flexible cluster-robust estimators that can accommodate any user-defined estimator. Our results show that the proposed estimators outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy in simulated scenarios. Additionally, we provide real-world examples to demonstrate the practical application and benefits of the new estimators. Our new method can be easily implemented using the R package pairedData.

A novel, time-step control approach has been developed to accelerate the numerical simulation of complex fluid flows that involve the complex interactions of multiple phases. This algorithm involves a integration method that utilizes varying time steps across different parts of the simulation and in various spatial domains. By dividing the simulation into various modules, each with its own time step and by using a customized force calculation approach, the methods of fast computation can be applied more effectively. This approach has been successfully used to accelerate the simulation of particle-laden flows and has shown significant speed improvements over traditional methods.

The BHWKI protocol demonstrates that without additional information, defining particles in relation to an evaporating black hole yields a nonsensical outcome, implying an infinitely large particle count emitted during evaporation. To resolve this apparent contradiction, we argue that the BHWKI experiment setup doesn't truly result in particle emission, but rather entangles the emitted particle with the black hole's remnants. We propose a modified version of the BHWKI experiment in which both particles and black hole remnants are collected, and show that after gathering all evaporation byproducts, a defined particle emission can indeed be identified.

Using the CGC model, we investigate the influence of varying dipole cross-section models on predictions of nuclear broadening in high-energy collisions. Our analysis compares the EPS09 and EIKOR optical models of nuclear parton distribution functions with ALICE experimental data for Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions. Additionally, we examine the effectiveness of two different models for calculating dipole interactions, namely the quark-dipole and nucleon-dipole models. Our results indicate that the EPA-based distribution of nucleon dipoles significantly improves agreement between the model and experimental data compared to quark distributions.

We demonstrate that the equation $7^{\mathtt{n}}=a^3+2b^3$ has infinitely many solutions for the variable $\mathtt{n}$ with positive integers $a$ and $b$. Additionally, it has been proven that the equation $7^{\mathtt{n}}=a^3+2b^3$ only has the solution $\mathtt{a}=\mathtt{b}=0$ when $\mathtt{n}$ is a negative integer.

The influence of air on a liquid's behavior within a channel is examined through experiments and numerical simulations. The studies focus on how air entrainment affects the liquid's dynamics, particularly in relation to surface tension and viscous effects. Two distinct regimes are identified, and it is found that at low surface tension or high air entrainment, the differences between air and liquid densities become irrelevant to the system's behavior.

The incorporation of non-volatile memory in systems enables faster access to persistent data, making it an attractive option for numerous architectures. However, the incorporation of this type of memory in systems poses significant challenges in preserving data consistency, given its lack of a unified global ordering mechanism. To address this issue, many systems have been developed, but they often require the installation of specialized hardware or sophisticated operating systems. To overcome this, we developed an efficient algorithm that can be implemented in software within Linux environments, ensuring that shared data remains consistent even in the event of unexpected system crashes. This algorithm was integrated into C++ applications and tested in various scenarios, including different types of system crashes and data retrieval operations. Our results show that the algorithm efficiently maintains data consistency across different failure scenarios and retrieval operations, while also providing a unified ordering mechanism for data, thereby enabling concurrent data access and modification by multiple threads.

Networks of documents can uncover hidden relationships between texts that are often obscured from humans, but statistical methods may struggle with their complexity and volume. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model, a novel technique that reveals the interconnected structure of document networks. This model combines traditional topic modeling with a model of how documents relate to each other, employing a non-parametric approach to detect clusters without prior assumptions. We compare our method to popular techniques, including those used in clustering and visualizing documents, using a dataset of news articles, and demonstrate that HDTM effectively reveals meaningful structures in complex document networks.

This research delves into the intricacies of chaotic escape in three-body systems, examining its quantitative aspects through detailed numerical analysis. We have investigated the Frye and Lacey model, assessing whether existing predictions align with actual systems in three-body interactions. Additionally, we explored the relationship between orbital periods and escape probabilities at various thresholds, also considering the impact of initial energy levels on escape probabilities. Our findings indicate that system quantities are consistent with expected outcomes, also revealing that high-energy systems exhibit greater escape possibilities, particularly for intermediate quantities, contrary to low-energy systems which tend to match lower-energy characteristics.

A study of the suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons in comparison to $J/\psi$ mesons across different transverse momentum ranges, from 2 to 100 $GeV/c$, is presented. The data was collected using the CMS experiment at the LHC with $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 $TeV$. The relative suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons in the lower transverse momentum range is found to be lower than that of $J/\psi$ mesons. However, at transverse momenta above 10 $GeV/c$, $\psi$(2S) $T_{\rm{R}}$-factor values are found to be close to unity, suggesting a transition from a complex medium interaction to the $pp$ environment. This transition occurs at a transverse momentum of approximately 10 $GeV/c$, which is about 10 times the $\psi$(2S) mass. The observed patterns are in line with predictions from perturbative QCD calculations at NLO.

In continuous logic, equivalence relations are represented as complete metric spaces with specific distances, and we explore how to model complete spaces with multiple equivalence classes under specific conditions. Our approach focuses on defining distances between different equivalence classes and we establish criteria for when these models are isometric to others. Specifically, we examine situations where every equivalence class in one model corresponds exactly to every equivalence class in another model. Our analysis is particularly relevant to continuous logic, where equivalence relations are common, and we demonstrate the model-theoretic distances' applications in this context.

One effective approach to managing changes in complex software systems involves
leveraging a simple metric to identify and remove unnecessary components that no
longer contribute to the system's current configuration. Although widely used in
data compression and error reduction techniques, applying this metric to track
software evolution poses a significant challenge due to the absence of a clear
interpretation of its individual values in the context of software systems. In
this research, we investigate the application of metric-based refactoring techniques
to identify and monitor meaningful changes in software architectures over time.
Our methodology utilizes matrix operations to synthesize and analyze the evolution
of related software modules, enabling the detection of emerging modules through
singular value decomposition. Our approach has been successfully applied to the
publicly available Linux kernel projects, where it has helped to track the
integration of related modules and their subsequent separation into distinct
projects.

Deep sequential models like RNNs and LSTMs are highly effective at modeling complex sequences, but they can struggle with long sequences due to vanishing gradients and high computational costs. In this research, we integrate an attention-based framework into an existing long-sequence RNN model for time-series classification. By limiting RNN connections and using an attention-based weighted system, we enable efficient processing of extended sequences. Our proposed attention-LSTM model surpasses the performance of the baseline LSTM and existing state-of-the-art models on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets.

Cassiopeia A, a remnant of a stellar explosion, exhibits intense emission across various wavelengths, with notable features including rapidly moving shell structures and a complex, multi-loop structure in the polarized X-ray emission. The emission's origin is believed to be linked to the shock wave interacting with the surrounding material, while the field's orientation is likely influenced by the magnetic field within that material. A detailed examination of the X-ray emission's total and polarized intensity, along with its relationship to radio observations, has led to a significant discovery. It has been found that the six main loops in the emission are aligned with the magnetic field, with a field angle of approximately 110 degrees, with angular differences of only 10-20 degrees. This remarkable alignment suggests a shared origin for the material in both the E and W lobes, with the material likely originating from a source within a spiral-shaped structure.

Poonen and Rubinstein's research found that a random unique subset sum instance with n elements and a range of size O(n^2) has a probability approaching zero of containing a subset with distinct sums. We build on this finding by presenting two key results. Firstly, we build on these research findings and discover that a range of O(n^2 / log n) is sufficient for the mentioned probability to approach zero when considering subsets of size up to a third of the total number of elements. Secondly, we demonstrate that a range of O(n^2) is sufficient for the mentioned probability to approach zero when there are no subset distinct sum constraints and the subset size can be up to half of the total number of elements.

The study of compact stars, particularly quark stars, is an active field of research.
Recent X-ray observations of neutron stars have led to the development of new
constraints on the properties of the star's internal matter.
We present a simplified model of a star containing a deconfinement phase transition
and investigate its effect on the mass-radius relationship.
By applying our model to the star PSR J1748-+2456CD, the most massive known star,
we derive an upper limit for its radius of 12.6 km.
This upper limit is significantly influenced by the properties of the phase transition.

We investigate the use of the compass state, a highly entangled N-qubit state, in quantum metrology for estimating a damping parameter $\gamma$. The complexity of the compass state can be adjusted by changing the parameter $\theta$, allowing us to explore how its structure affects performance. Our research reveals that the most intricate compass states exhibit the lowest number variance and consequently have limited usefulness in estimating small values of $\gamma$. Conversely, the simplicity of these states improves their accuracy in larger $\gamma$ ranges. Notably, our findings reveal that the optimal states exhibit lower complexity, leading to easier state preparation and more reliable estimation. The presence of negative discrete rank in the density matrix of these optimal states also indicates the presence of significant entanglement.

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to describe the geometry of a liquid jet in motion. This model is validated against experimental observations of a liquid jet produced by a falling stream from a tube with a small opening. It is also capable of explaining distinct types of jets with different geometries and offers a theoretical basis for their classification. Furthermore, the model is consistent with the existing understanding of dynamic behavior in jets, and it provides a simplified explanation for the formation of cones and cylinders. This theoretical framework can be applied to predict the properties of other moving liquid jets.

Observations of viruses moving in a rolling motion have been made in previous studies, 
but the underlying physics of this motion have never been successfully explained. 
By examining slow-motion videos of bacteriophages during their interaction with bacteria, 
it is discovered that the rolling motion arises from the uneven contraction of tail fibers, 
caused by the sequential release of tension during retraction. 
The sequence in which the fibers contract also varies from one instance to another. 
To explain this motion, a model is developed in which the bending of the virus's body 
is driven by the metabolic processes occurring on its surface. 
Interestingly, the virus doesn't need to absorb nutrients to exhibit this behavior, 
as the'substrates' that create tension and drive motion are the virus's own surface components.

Our research focuses on the distinct characteristics of U and S type galaxy warps and their underlying causes. Although the majority of studies have concentrated on S type warped galaxies, our analysis reveals that U type warped galaxies exhibit similar warp properties. Furthermore, our findings indicate that U and S type warped galaxies are subject to different environmental influences, with U type warped galaxies experiencing stronger tidal forces from their neighbors and a higher likelihood of interacting with a nearby galaxy within half their diameter. In contrast, S type warped galaxies are often found in regions with lower tidal forces and are less likely to have close galaxy encounters. Moreover, our analysis shows that U and S type warped galaxies are affected differently by dark matter distribution, with S type warped galaxies being more likely to reside in regions where dark matter is concentrated in the inner regions, whereas U type warped galaxies are more likely to have a uniform dark matter distribution.

This communication employs a harmonic function with exponential growth to demonstrate that certain classes of gradient shrinking Ricci solitons are compact under specific conditions. Our approach generalizes and expands upon a previously established result obtained by S. M. Bakry and Z. Qian.

To investigate the phase symmetry breaking in KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, we studied the effects of doping and strain using first-principles calculations. In doping, we found that in KRbBi$_{4}$, replacing potassium with rubidium preserves its phase symmetry, whereas replacing rubidium with potassium leads to lattice distortion and phase symmetry breaking. However, straining the crystal in KRbBi$_{4}$ can break its phase symmetry without doping. In contrast, in RbCsBi$_{4}$, replacing the potassium ion with a rubidium ion leads to phase symmetry breaking, whereas straining the crystal maintains its phase symmetry. Moreover, we discovered that in RbCsBi$_{4}$, replacing the rubidium ion with a potassium ion leads to phase symmetry breaking, whereas straining the crystal preserves its phase symmetry. Our research indicates that phase symmetry breaking in KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$ can be induced by doping or strain, providing an alternative approach to creating multiferroic materials.

The application of polar effective charges is a widely used method for describing charge transport. In clean, nonmagnetic insulators, these effective charges can be understood through band structure perturbations, but the same approach breaks down in conductors due to the presence of scattering. The same limitation applies to the BZ-Integrated nonadiabatic current, but the situation is more complex with BZ-resolved quantities. Our research reveals that in clean conductors, transport-related current components conform to a sum rule that is analogous to an insulator model, whereas they diverge significantly from a BZ-averaged current definition. The latter diverges notably from its insulator counterpart, specifically in the case of monochromatic electron distributions. The findings suggest that the effective charge formalism may be expanded upon to describe the charge-charge interaction in conductors.

The fluctuating hydrodynamics equations are derived to describe the stochastic behavior of turbulent fluid flow at a mesoscopic scale, accounting for random forces and the fluctuating nature of the flow. Our research compares the deterministic Navier-Stokes equations with the fluctuating hydrodynamics equations and identifies a significant difference in their energy balance equations. Specifically, the balance equations for the two models are found to be distinct, with the stochastic model exhibiting an additional non-stationary term. This term represents the random energy fluctuations inherent in turbulent flow and cannot be ignored. As a result, the energy dissipation rate in the fluctuating model exhibits stochastic behavior, in contrast to the deterministic model. These findings highlight the importance of considering random forces and energy fluctuations when studying and modeling turbulent fluid flow.

A key indicator of magnetoelectric (ME) coupling in magnetic solids is the Thirring effect, characterized by an electric charge that appears when an electric dipole is induced in a magnetic monopole when it is passed through the material's bulk. We have found that this Witten effect can also occur with quasi-monic ions in certain ternary compounds that exhibit a THz mode at the $\Gamma$ point. These compounds have an ABC structure where the interaction between ions at sites A and B mimics the interaction between an electron and a monopole in a spin-1 system. We have identified two such compounds, YTiO$_4$ and LuTiO$_4$, in which the electron transfer between quasi-monopoles leads to a charge that appears when an electron is moved through the material's bulk in response to an applied DC magnetic field. This effect can be observed through changes in photoconductivity in optical experiments that track the absorption of energy carried by DC electric fields generated by external batteries.
