Cotangent bundles in symplectic manifolds with no sections present lead to unique expressions for curvature weights, which in turn enable the identification of a set of curvatures with minimal ranks.

In chains governed by Hertzian nonlinearity, two exponentially weak oscillations arise due to coupling between motion along the chain and perpendicular to it. We demonstrate that, when the chain is finite, these oscillations can combine to create very weak, yet detectable, solitary waves. We examine how the size of these oscillations depends on factors such as the mass per unit, the spacing between particles, the temperature, and the initial energy input. We also explore the impact of random disturbances on these oscillations and find that their effect is minimal. We explore two scenarios for creating these oscillations: one where they are created by moving the chain back and forth at a low rate, and another where they are created by striking the chain at a low velocity.

The complex structure of the primordial universe is a major focus of research in cosmology. A key area of study within this field is the statistical measure of non-uniformity in the early universe, referred to as $f_{NL}$. A more comprehensive understanding of this statistical property, known as the Maldacen non-Gaussianity framework, is necessary to gain deeper insights into the early universe. A crucial parameter in this analysis is the spectral tilt of the primordial fluctuations, $\eta$. A more precise measurement of $\eta$ will provide a deeper understanding of the early universe's formation and evolution. A more accurate measurement of $\eta$ will also shed light on the non-uniform distribution of matter in the early universe. A more precise measurement of $\eta$ will also provide a deeper understanding of the early universe's formation and evolution. A more accurate measurement of $\eta$ will also provide a deeper understanding of the early universe's formation and evolution.

The accordion graph class $A[n,k]$ is an interconnected combination of two types of graphs, specifically the complete graph and the cycle graph. By examining the eigenvectors of this graph type, we can determine its spectrum and identify under what conditions it is or isn't considered a circulant graph. When the parameter $k$ equals one of two values, either $n-1$ or $1$, the class $A[n,k]$ is not a circulant graph. Otherwise, it is a circulant graph, with its spectrum consisting of two sets of distinct eigenvalues, each with its own multiplicity.

We've developed a theoretical framework to analyze the long-term behavior of a quantum walk on a graph with an embedded defect. The framework involves representing the dynamics on this modified graph as a unitary UMF on a space formed by the sum of two other spaces, one representing the graph minus the defect and the other representing the defect itself. We've found that near a specific angle, known as the detrapping angle, the dynamics change significantly. On the modified graph minus the defect, the dynamics become non-ergodic, while the ratio of participation changes from linear to quadratic growth in a neighborhood of this angle. Moreover, we've found that the participation changes exhibit a continuous transition, moving from a linear to quadratic growth in a neighborhood of the detrapping angle.

Self-supervised learning techniques have become crucial in training high-quality visual models without requiring labeled data. In our experiment, we investigated the effectiveness of self-supervised methods in pre-training Vision Transformers (ViT) on the ImageNet dataset. Notably, we found that the DINO self-supervision technique, which involves masked image modeling and entropy regularization, significantly outperformed other methods like MoCo and ViTLS. Specifically, with just 85 cropped images per class, the pre-trained DINO model achieved a 76.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, surpassing the pre-trained ViT by 5.1%. Moreover, the DINO pre-trained model also exhibited exceptional zero-shot performance on diverse datasets, including CIFAR-100, Country2Country, Stanford Online, JFT-30M, WebVision, and Stanford Cars.

A modified version of the $\Lambda$CDM model is explored in this review, incorporating the idea of viscosity in cosmology. By utilizing the Bianchi type III metric, we derive a model that offers a novel interpretation of dark energy and dark matter. Our analysis focuses on the model's implications for the universe's evolution, revealing a viscosity coefficient that declines over time. Specifically, the viscosity is highest during the matter-dominated era and drops to zero as the universe transitions to a $\Lambda$-dominated state, aligning with the model's assumption of zero viscosity in late cosmological times. Our findings are supported by observational data from Type Ia Supernovae and the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation, indicating the model is consistent with current measurements.

In incompressible Euler equations, the occurrence of smooth solutions with arbitrary small amplitude is confirmed. It is also established that smooth solutions with arbitrary small amplitude are possible when considering $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \geq 3$ or $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a specific weighted Sobolev space for a given constant $\gamma \in (-1,1)$. The solutions are made possible by leveraging a family of vector fields that are divergence-free and converge to the boundary, as well as a non-linear transformation that maps the unit disk to a simply connected domain.

Building on prior research, we introduce 'Stable Artist', an interface that integrates the strengths of text and brush-based inputs within a unified framework, addressing a balance between controllability and creativity. Our model, rooted in a theoretical approach, allows for the co-existence of multiple control modalities without one overshadowing the other. User studies demonstrate that Stable Artist improves the experience of text-only models by providing more direct and user-friendly control, while its artist component fosters creativity. Additionally, we introduce 'Stable Diffusion with Dynamics', an extension of the Stable Diffusion model, which incorporates motion capture data to enable users to control virtual artists in the image generation process, resulting in more dynamic and engaging images.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in processing and analyzing complex data, yet their deployment in critical applications such as medicine and law enforcement is hindered by their unexplained uncertainty. A more transparent and trustworthy AI system is necessary to address this issue. Although probabilistic methods have been developed to quantify the uncertainty in neural networks, they have yet to be applied to training data to identify batches that increase model uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach that incorporates Bayesian uncertainty into batch selection during training to identify data batches that improve model reliability. Our method utilizes Relevance and Uncertainty weights to control the influence of individual data points on the model's performance. By applying our approach to image classification tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying data batches that enhance model reliability without compromising accuracy.

The presence of dark matter may manifest in experiments searching for dark matter at the Large Hadron Collider as a signal of missing energy. Such searches are influenced by the background noise created by the decay of certain particles into non-visible matter, including the top quark, $W$ boson, and the $J/\psi$ charmonium. In addition to examining the overall rate of events in these searches, individual analyses of final states can also be conducted. In this paper, we investigate how the $J/\psi$ decay into non-visible matter affects the accuracy of measurements taken by the ATLAS and CMS experiments in examining how dark matter scatters off nucleons. We found that excluding $J/\psi$ events can significantly improve the sensitivity of these searches, with cross-sectional limits increasing by up to an order of magnitude in some cases. In addition, we demonstrate that removing $J/\psi$ events can also lead to more precise measurements of overall event rates, with statistical uncertainties reduced by as much as 20%.

A thorough examination of magnetic bright points in a solar active region has been conducted through statistical analysis of their motion and velocity components. Researchers used data from the SDO/AIA telescope to track magnetic bright points in two distinct wavelengths, focusing on their movement and change over time. This study found that the movement of magnetic bright points in different directions follows distinct patterns, with their movements in each direction being statistically independent of one another. Moreover, the study revealed that the movement of magnetic bright points in each direction is not normally distributed, with their overall movement being the result of multiple distinct motions. These findings have significant implications for understanding the role of magnetic bright points in driving solar phenomena such as surges and their connection to moving flux and reconnection processes.

Human-like robots need advanced visual skills to navigate and operate in their environment. A key area of development for these robots is dynamic vision, which enables them to interpret and respond to moving objects in real-time. A challenge that arises is creating a dataset of diverse, yet concise, videos that effectively train and test the visual perception of robots. This paper presents a new dataset consisting of 1000 objects, each featuring a set of 10 minimal videos that showcase different aspects of their motion. These minimal videos are designed to be both informative and efficient, enabling the robots to learn and adapt to new objects with high accuracy. Our analysis shows that the minimal dataset performs comparably to larger, more complex datasets, while significantly reducing the amount of data required for accurate object recognition.

We've discovered new bound monopole ground states in a three-dimensional $SU(2)$ Yang-Mills--Proca theory with massive abelian photons. These monopoles can be effectively described as $U(1)$ magnetic dipoles having both a north and a south component. The north component exhibits attractive behavior, while the south component exhibits a repulsive force, similar to ordinary magnetic dipoles. As a result, the bound monopole's energy and size are heavily influenced by its oriented magnetic moment. When placed in a magnetic field, the bound monopole's stability is greatly enhanced. Additionally, magnetic fields can cause the bound monopole's energy to become positive, leading to its dissolution into free monopoles and antimonopoles.

Deep learning has become a leading approach for weather forecasting due to its superior performance compared to traditional numerical methods. However, the effectiveness of deep learning models is heavily influenced by the way the weather data is formatted and processed. We conducted an extensive study to determine the impact of dataset preparation on weather prediction accuracy. We investigated the effects of scaling the weather data and the use of multiple channels to represent atmospheric conditions. We evaluated these effects on two widely used neural network models, ScaledConv2D and U-Net, using a rigorous statistical analysis. We discovered that normalizing the dataset has a significant impact on Conv2D models, but not on spatial transformer models. Furthermore, we found that dataset preparation can alter the optimal hyperparameter settings and the stability of the models. We also examined the impact of input data organization on another Conv2D model, ScaledConv2D, and found that both "3 weather data channels + 1 control variable" and "4 weather data channels" configurations are viable. We found that these results align with the observed behavior of atmospheric dynamics, particularly the relationship between pressure and temperature. We found that these results are consistent with the observed behavior of atmospheric conditions, such as the relationship between pressure and temperature.

Within the framework of a specific theoretical model, we investigate dark matter interactions. The model consists of three interacting particle groups and their relationship to dark matter is examined. By analyzing the model's potential, we determine the conditions required for the dark matter to interact correctly with normal particles. These conditions are then used to identify the range of possible dark matter masses, which, due to complex particle relationships, can vary widely from very light to very heavy. Additionally, we analyze how likely dark matter to be detected in particle colliders, taking into account possible particle combinations. Our analysis shows that changing particle relationships significantly affects detection likelihood, potentially making very heavy dark matter detectable in future colliders.

The self-assembly of tubulin dimers into microtubules is a fundamental biological process that underpins the formation of the cytoskeleton in living organisms. The structural properties of these dimers dictate the morphology of the resulting microtubules, which in turn influence the efficient delivery of nutrients to brain cells. Our research explores the optimal alignment of tubulin dimers within a one-dimensional lattice to maximize the fraction of defective bonds, thereby facilitating transport. By applying a combination of combinatorial methods and advanced algorithms, we've developed a generalized approach to address this challenge across a broad range of scenarios, ultimately revealing a set of structural configurations that enable efficient nutrient delivery across various latice sizes.

In the realm of banking, graph-based machine learning has proven effective in identifying fraudulent activities. As a result, financial institutions are increasingly employing graph neural networks to analyze banking transactions. However, due to confidentiality concerns, real transaction data cannot be shared for training and evaluation purposes. While existing approaches attempt to create synthetic graphs by generating fake vertices and edges, they often overlook the hierarchical structure inherent in banking transactions. This paper presents an innovative framework for hierarchical graph synthesis in banking environments. Our framework utilizes the Tail-Head Graph framework to model tail-to-tail relationships and a Poisson process for edge synthesis. A novel approach is developed to ensure the generated graphs adhere to 2-hop patterns found in real banking transactions. The efficacy of our framework is demonstrated through its ability to replicate key characteristics of actual transaction data, including the distribution of graph density and centralization, as well as the Gini index.

In the process of merging between a black hole and a stellar companion, the lost mass from the stellar companion's mass loss can result in the creation of an accretion disc around the black hole, potentially leading to unique and observable characteristics in the ultraviolet to X-ray spectrum.

The study of CP symmetry violations in three-body tau decays can be approached
through an analysis of angular distributions of final-state particles.
Investigations into these CP violations are particularly relevant in the context
of three-neutrino oscillations, as they can be explored via studies of hadronic
tau decays. In hadronic decay chains, the secondary vertices resulting from
hadron decays provide crucial information for analyzing CP violations.
Future research facilities, such as the Intensity Frontier projects, will be
able to analyze data with high precision, enabling a detailed examination of
these phenomena.

We investigate the geometric characteristics of the convex cone formed by metrics described by the "symmetric Tversberg ratio models" with parameters ranging between zero and one. These models are widely used to create a customizable family of metrics derived from a base "non-metric function." We identify the boundary of this cone, the extreme points, its boundary, and its shape, providing insights into the relationship between the parameters and the function that define the model.

This paper introduces a novel, highly effective deblurring framework that consists of two key components: a primary module for feature extraction and a specialized reblurring module. The feature extraction module utilizes a pre-trained deep network to generate initial features from blurry inputs, which are then processed by the reblurring module to produce a preliminary blurry image. A loss function comparing the residual between the preliminary blurry image and the original input refines the network's parameters. The reblurring module's interplay with the feature extraction module enhances deburring performance by preventing information loss during deburring processes. Additionally, our framework's loss function incorporates high-frequency components, further contributing to its inter effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing techniques in multiple assessments, and our source code will be available on GitHub.

Recent research has revealed that certain patterns of autonomous learning in chemical reaction networks (CRNs) mirror similar behavior observed in neurons. A critical question arises: can we devise an algorithm to translate any learning rule that involves input and internal variables into a specific type of dynamical system, including CRNs, that retells any given learning process? The answer lies in developing a novel algorithm that generates a dynamic system, composed of reversible and multiplicative CRNs, that models polynomial learning rules taking multiple inputs and featuring multiplicative neuromodulation. The created system, which is multiplicative CRN-friendly, is based on a new class of networks that are known to be efficiently simulatable through standard means.

We investigate the concept of original-completeness in the context of nonstandard analysis. This is done by extending work of T. Slater on ultrapowers of dense sets. T. Slater demonstrated that if a set is countable and nonstandardly bounded, its ultrapower can be closed through a process of saturation. We show that the properties of density and nonstandard-boundedness are essential to Slater's result. Consequently, we establish that original-completeness is an intrinsic property of the underlying set. Furthermore, we prove that original-completeness is equivalent to a specific property involving countable sets. This leads to the conclusion that the majority of sets are not original-complete. In addition, we explore the properties of original-completeness in relation to various standard sets, including the standard reals, integers, rational numbers, natural numbers, and the natural scale.

In the field of data-driven science, scientists are tasked with exploring large datasets to uncover hidden patterns, but data analysis tools are often too computationally intensive to be used on a larger scale. Our goal is to address this challenge by developing an efficient data analysis framework that can be applied to data-driven science. We've incorporated two key components into our framework - an accurate data analytics pipeline based on statistical theory and a K8s-based cloud infrastructure that facilitates benchmarking. By leveraging cloud computing, we can improve the precision of benchmarking through high-performance data analytics code execution. Our approach also enables flexible and efficient resource allocation, allowing users to set custom time and resource limits for code submissions, thus enabling cost-effective analytics submissions.

A 1992 hypothesis by Chernikova proposed that every graph G with t chromatic numbers containing a t-complete (K_t) substructure could be replaced with another t chromatic graph consisting of t connected components. The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate the incorrectness of this hypothesis by constructing two distinct counterexamples: (1) a 3 chromatic graph with a 3 complete (K_3) substructure that does not have a 3 complete (K_3) connected component, and (2) a 4 chromatic graph with a 4 complete (K_4) substructure that does not have a 4 complete (K_4) connected component. The second counterexample involves the use of the Moser spindle, specifically designed for chromatic numbers of 4.

The performance of an adaptive algorithm operating in environments with noisy inputs and shifting conditions is examined. The behavior of the algorithm is modeled as a discrete-time stochastic process. The study considers cost functions with varying degrees of convexity and noise levels. The results show that as noise levels increase, the algorithm's ability to find optimal solutions diminishes, particularly for cost functions with minimal convexity. The theoretical findings are validated through simulations.

The collision-cycling rate is adjusted by changing the optical cavity's coupling to the surrounding environment. The optical Cavity-QED system consists of a series of two-level atoms that move in a specific pattern and interact with a specific type of light within an adjustable optical cavity. The entangling collisions produce a specific, entangled state of atoms that can be adjusted by changing the collision-cycling rate. The entangled state of atoms in a Cavity-QED system has specific properties that can be used for precise measurements of specific types of forces and can be used for the creation of specific types of light for specific measurements of specific types of particles. The research shows that the optimal condition for the production of highly entangled atomic collisions in a Cavity-QED system can be adjusted by changing the collision-cycling rate. The collision-cycling rate is the rate at which the entangled collisions occur in a Cavity-QED system. The optimal condition for the production of highly entangled atomic collisions in a Cavity-QED system is the condition at which the collision-cycling rate is the same as the rate of loss of photons in the cavity. We explore the behavior of the $p$-Laplacian under a specific nonlinear boundary condition, denoted by $u^{p-1}=\alpha |u|^{\beta-1}u$ on a given bounded domain in $R^p$. By defining a parameter $\alpha$ based on the first Robin eigenvalue $\lambda_1$, we determine under what conditions this eigenvalue remains unique and maintain its positivity. Building upon previous research, we define a class of functions that help us derive lower and upper bounds for $\lambda_1$, which are expressed in terms of the domain's geometric properties.

Building on existing research, this work explores the connections between traditional Convolutional Neural Networks and fully connected Neural Networks, and demonstrates how they can be viewed as specific cases of Graph Convolutional Networks. Additionally, this paper investigates GCNs' applicability to image recognition tasks, and compares their performance with conventional CNNs.

This research introduces an enhanced contextualized self-training algorithm, referred to as Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), which builds upon the principles of previous self-training methods. Unlike its predecessors, DCST can capitalize on the full potential of neural network architectures. The proposed algorithm is particularly effective when applied to pre-trained models and demonstrates significant improvements in various parsing tasks, including dependency parsing, constituent parsing, and coreference resolution. Notably, DCST achieves substantial gains when using models with limited or no training data, and its performance rivals that of SOTA self-supervised learning methods when employing a moderate amount of labeled data. The source code for DCST will be made available on GitHub.

Using proton-proton collision data collected at high energies by the LHCb experiment, we've analyzed the decay of B mesons into D mesons in combination with either a lepton (electron, muon, or tau) and a neutrino, or with a lepton, neutrino, and a jet. Our analysis, which accounts for the limited detection capabilities for tau leptons, reveals that the ratio of branching ratios between tau and muon modes is 3.8 times the predicted Standard Model value, with significant deviation, whereas the ratio between muon and electron modes aligns with expectations, showing no significant deviation. Additionally, we found that the product of two such branching ratios is 1.5 times the predicted Standard Model value, with significant deviation.

A comprehensive approach to identifying and calculating properties of non-invertible symmetries is presented, grounded in concepts from gauge, duality, and tensor network theory. By connecting these ideas to established concepts such as anomaly free extensions and the splitting of dualities into simple components, we establish a framework for classifying non-invertible symmetries and deriving their fusion rules. This approach also enables the calculation of non-invertible operator correlation functions through renormalization group flow, which in turn provides insights into symmetry defect operator identities. This formalism is applied to explore the properties of $1+1$-dimensional gauge theories, including abelian and non-abelian cases like $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory and SU($N$) gauge theory, as well as conformal field theories with global symmetry.

We are examining an important problem in finite field mathematics. Given an unordered linear equation system with coefficients and a non-zero constant, we want to determine if a solution exists for the system. Specifically, for which prime numbers p does a solution exist become a computationally definable property in the language of logic with only a few symbols. This problem has a positive answer when p is a prime number greater than or equal to 5, but we provide acombinatorial proof that it is definable when p is the prime number 3.

The crystal structure and magnetic properties of (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir_2O_7 were investigated using X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. Our results indicate that Bi substitution preserves the original crystal structure but introduces a larger unit cell. Analysis of Bi's valence band shows increased spectral intensity, suggesting a higher concentration of Bi in the material. Our XPS data also reveal that Bi substitution causes a shift in the 710 eV peak towards lower binding energy, which is consistent with the incorporation of Bi in the layers. Our findings suggest that Bi substitution expands the material's crystal structure and modifies its electronic properties.

We establish a new theorem on the existence of Lipschitzian selections for set-valued mappings defined on a complete metric space, taking nonempty, convex, and closed subsets of a Banach space as values. This new result generalizes and extends previously established thorems in this area. The proof relies on a novel and distinct approach. The theorem is then applied to demonstrate the existence of optimal solutions for certain optimization problems involving distance functions defined on subset-valued mappings over complete metric spaces.

Given real numbers from 0 to 1, the n-tuple (p1 through pn) is nontransitive when there's one number that is greater than another number chosen randomly from the remaining n-1 numbers for all possible combinations. We'll derive a specific condition to determine whether an n-tuple is nontransitive.

A run-time option allows users to adjust software behavior according to their needs.
However, options can be disabled at compile-time, which is often done to save space or improve security.
While this practice is common, it can be confusing when an option is disabled but still appears available to users.
In this research, we examine the impact of removing disabled run-time options on an operating system's size, security, and overall performance.
By analyzing the kernel of Linux, we found that compile-time disabled options can still have a significant impact on the system's size and security.
In some cases, an option may not directly affect system size but can provide access to functions that do have an impact.
Additionally, we discovered that an option can be compile-time disabled but still have functions available to be used at run-time.
In contrast to our findings, an analysis of an option-rich system, NetBSD, showed that most compile-time disabled options have little to no impact on system size and security.
However, an option can still have functions available to be used even if it is compile-time disabled.
Based on these results, we have developed an approach to automatically identify functions that are not used, which can then be removed to improve system size and security.
In testing, we found that over 20% of kernel code in Linux and over 10% in NetBSD were unnecessary and could be removed.

The ionisation of noble liquids by dark matter is an important indicator for its detection.  SnowCube, a large-volume Cherenkov neutrino detector, is being designed to also search for dark matter through supertons of ionised liquid argon.  SnowCube's design involves a series of 10-m diameter, 60-m long cylinders filled with liquid argon and sealed with stainless steel.  Due to the steel's suppression of ionisation, SnowCube's sensitivity to nuclear recoil events is primarily affected by dark matter-lectron interactions.  This study explores the degree to which dark matter-lectron interactions can limit SnowCube's ability to detect dark matter, with findings suggesting that its reach may be comparable to other leading direct detection experiments.

In this research, we have developed a sophisticated technique for transferring information about spin orientation over short distances using low-energy quantum systems. The process involves using the principles of 'anti-polariton qubits' to achieve this goal. The access to unique quantum states of light-matter interaction allows us to develop novel quantum communication methods. The experiments show that our approach can maintain a high level of fidelity, even when separated by a distance of several hundred nanometers. The proposed method has the potential to be used in the development of complex quantum circuits and networks. The research also demonstrates the ability to perform high-fidelity quantum gate operations between anti-polariton qubits, as well as measure and verify the entanglement between them using a specialized form of Bell's inequality. The findings have significant implications for the advancement of quantum information processing technologies.

Deep-learning techniques have significantly advanced the accuracy of extracting heart rate information from heart signals by effectively dealing with real-world issues such as signal discontinuities and added noise. A new method involves combining two neural networks to process and align segments of heart signals, which are then used to create and refine predictions on R-waves, ultimately improving the accuracy of inter-beat interval estimation. This technique was tested against existing methods and demonstrated better performance in determining the location of R-waves and calculating inter-beat intervals.

Active systems governed by non-linear forces exhibit unique properties that set them apart from their passive counterparts. To better understand systems governed by active forces, we developed and tested models that simulate these systems in different potential environments - both harmonic and anharmonic - and compared them in two dimensions. Our research focused on the distribution of energy and fluctuations within these systems. We discovered that, similar to passive systems, harmonic systems exhibit optimal behavior at specific points, whereas anharmonic systems do not follow this pattern. Our findings also revealed that, unlike passive systems, harmonic and active systems do not obey certain established relationships, such as the equipartition theorem, in all cases. To gain a deeper understanding of these systems, we developed methods to analyze and interpret their energy spectra, providing valuable insights into the underlying dynamics.

HUMBI is a novel approach that utilizes a generative 3D model to translate human facial expressions from a neutral state to various other emotions, maintaining consistency across multiple views. As an extension of Neural SDFs, which represent real objects in 3D space, we integrate this technique with SMX-FF, a method that encodes facial expression movements as conditional SDFs. This integration enables us to perform SDF modulation in order to achieve consistent and expressive facial transformations in real time. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our approach produces highly realistic and view-consistent emotional expressions in real human faces, and successfully applies this technology to the metaverse.

Developing a single model that can accurately translate between multiple languages is a desirable goal, but it is hindered by the scarcity of translation data and the limited translation paths available in current language pairs. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a new framework that leverages the translation invariance of different languages to train a translation model across many languages simultaneously. By incorporating a new regularization term that maintains the compactness of a multi-language embedding space and allowing each language to contribute equally to the model's training, we are able to achieve accurate translations for languages with labeled data as well as those without. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing improved performance over baseline methods and state-of-the-art techniques in scenarios involving multiple language training and low-resource language settings.

BasicVSR++ is an enhanced version of BasicVSR with improved performance and efficiency. By integrating a cross-module connection and a compact decoder, BasicVSR++ achieves faster processing and lower memory consumption. Notably, it outperforms many current methods and achieves significant reductions in processing time and memory usage, with specific improvements of 0.42 PSNR and 10.12 MB, respectively, when compared to BasicVSR, while also surpassing SCNN by 0.44 PSNR and 12.06 MB.

In multi-task reinforcement learning environments, agents are often required to execute a variety of tasks that may share common characteristics but also have unique aspects.  To address this challenge, multi-task learning methods are employed to create a single, consolidated model of the environment's dynamics.  However, using one learned model can lead to incorrect assumptions about the environment's dynamics when applying it to tasks that were not part of the training set.  To tackle this issue, we introduce an agent that is capable of learning multiple, distinct models of the environment's dynamics, each tailored to tasks with similar characteristics.  We integrate a graph-based clustering method to automatically identify task groups and assign specific models to each.  Through a series of simulations, we demonstrate the benefits of this approach in terms of sample efficiency and task generalization.

A theoretical investigation examines the steady-state performance of a heat engine comprised of two heat baths and a small quantum system that can transition between two energy levels. The system's dynamics are influenced by two different heat bath models, characterized by harmonic oscillators in a large collective mode scenario, in conjunction with a quantum tunneling effect. One model employs a quantum master equation, while the other utilizes a Q factor method. Notably, the two approaches yield similar outcomes in most situations. The study reveals that, for both bath models, the tunneling effect can enhance the system's power output. Furthermore, it is found that increasing the system's coupling to the harmonic oscillators can also improve power output. Interestingly, it is found that adjusting a scaling parameter can optimize the heat engine's efficiency and power output, with an optimal point identified at this parameter's value of approximately 0.5.

Assessing the vulnerability of the US power grid to hurricanes is crucial for mitigating risks and ensuring resilience. This study employs Bayesian logic to create probabilistic hurricane impact scenarios, leveraging historical hurricane data and tracking records. By analyzing the characteristics of historical hurricanes that have affected the US power grid, the research identifies the most impactful hurricane types and develops corresponding scenarios. These scenarios are used to simulate the probability of grid outages and infrastructure damage, providing valuable insights for grid operators and policymakers. The findings are validated through the analysis of Hurricane Sandy's impact, demonstrating the accuracy of the developed models.
We develop a version of Hadamard's three circles theorem for monogenic functions, using the logarithmetic mean norm, in spaces of n dimensions.

We've developed a new type of piecewise affine maps, whose coding spaces are equivalent to the Dyck System, a well-known formal language that considers balanced parentheses as its foundational building blocks. This equivalence allows us to simplify complex problems within the realm of dynamical systems by reducing them to manageable combinatorial issues. Furthermore, our work demonstrates that the set of maps corresponding to the Dyck System forms a distinct subset within the broader population of all possible maps, whose size relative to the total population approaches zero as complexity increases.

A novel approach to developing finite state machines for modeling complex periodic signals, such as speech, involves utilizing a multi-layered structure where individual modules process single-layer information. Research has demonstrated that these machines can be effectively trained through backpropagation and have been applied successfully in tasks involving the modeling of nonverbal speech and the generation of corresponding vocalizations. Building on previous findings, this work presents a specific construction for these complex machines, provides an analysis of their computational complexity, and introduces an innovative training method combining greedy algorithm optimization with gradient-based techniques, which demonstrates improved results compared to training solely using the generalized backpropagation algorithm.

A novel USB Crowdsourcing platform called Fusion Biclustering Collaborative Filtering has been developed to enhance a recommendation system's accuracy by leveraging state-of-the-art biclustering techniques in Collaborative Filtering. This method's advantages lie in its ability to filter out noise from user ratings, reduce sparsity, and optimize computational efficiency. By introducing a novel biclustering approach that clusters users based on their rating patterns, users are divided into subgroups, allowing for more precise recommendations within each subgroup. This method's innovation lies in its ability to utilize only high-quality ratings from users who have rated the same items as above the average, thereby improving the reliability of recommendations. Experimental results using real-world datasets have shown that USB BCCF outperforms other biclustering-based CF methods in filtering noise, sparsity, and computational efficiency.

We have conducted a detailed examination of the star HD 69833, previously classified as a candidate host for an exoplanet, by analyzing its overall characteristics and magnetic activity. Utilizing data from the HARPS-N spectrograph, we analyzed 1100 high-quality spectra spanning 10 years. Our research involved measuring the star's overall activity through line asymmetry and equivalent width, and also explored specific indicators of activity within the HD 69833 spectrum. Our findings reveal that HD 69833 has an intermediate surface temperature of 5600K and rotational period of 12.6 days, and exhibits significant variability in brightness and line behavior, indicating a high level of activity. Our in-depth study confirms that HD 69833 is an active star and reveals that its signal may be influenced by stellar activity rather than the presence of an external object.

To investigate the local density of states at zero temperature in a hybrid nanostructure, we used tunneling spectroscopy to analyze a hybrid nanostructure at room temperature. The study involved a thin aluminum film coupled to a gold nanowire and measured the change in local density of states as temperature decreased. The data revealed that the local density of states at zero energy is influenced by non-Majorana effects and that this influence decreases with rising temperature, ultimately causing the zero-energy peak to disappear. We observed that the local density of states at zero temperature follows a specific relationship, where it is proportional to $(1-e^{-B_1/T})/(1-e^{-B_2/T})$ with positive constants $B_1$ and $B_2$. We developed two distinct models to fit the experimental data and found that both models are consistent with each other.

Consider a detailed investigation into the shadow of a bicategory in the context of topological spaces, showing that it corresponds to topological Hochschild homology (THH) within a structured framework of spaces and spaces over spaces. This discovery enables us to relate various instances of the shadow to familiar objects in the homotopy category of spaces. Furthermore, we derive a formula linking the THH-homology of a space to the shadow of a specific monoidal bicategory.

The concept of style and content in art has long been associated with distinguishing between artistic techniques and subject matter. In line with this distinction, recent research has attempted to separate style and content in images, however these studies have not thoroughly examined how learned representations actually capture artistic techniques versus content. We propose an novel approach to encoding images based on the assumption that content and style reside in separate subspaces. By applying this concept, we develop Gated-PC A (GPCA), an encoding technique that produces more accurate and robust representations compared to existing methods such as PCA or VAE. Furthermore, GPCA enables a content- and style-independent transformation of images, which we utilize to develop an algorithm for extracting artistic techniques from images. Our technique outperforms the current state-of-the-art in both qualitative and quantitative assessments, demonstrating its ability to effectively capture artistic techniques.

This research introduces a novel network architecture for video analysis, featuring 
perception, a context-ground module attention mechanism, and prediction components. 
The perception module utilizes two CNN-based encoders to extract spatio-temporal 
features, which are then combined through the attention mechanism utilizing previous 
frames and spatial locations. The contextual perception of multiple frames enables the 
network to effectively extract the most relevant information from them. The attention 
mechanism's input is generated using an efficient method that employs shared weights 
and ensures compatibility with a variety of network configurations. The prediction 
module employs a multi-head attention mechanism to integrate global feature information 
and enhance the network's forecasting capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate 
that this network outperforms existing methods in action recognition and video forecasting 
tasks, specifically MS-VID action recognition and MVLC video forecasting.

This research focuses on investigating how non-Newtonian fluids respond to constant shear stress, particularly in relation to snow particle behavior in dynamic conditions. To achieve this, we developed a model based on the discrete phase approach within a fully turbulent CFD framework. By integrating a new statistical model for snow particle velocity, we were able to simulate and analyze the settlement patterns of snow particles in turbulent environments. Our model demonstrates that settling speeds vary significantly based on the characteristics of snow particles, with higher particles exhibiting more predictable settling patterns. In contrast, lower particles show increased variability and often fail to settle due to their sensitivity to fluctuations in fluid velocity.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning techniques have significantly enhanced the capabilities of generative models to process high-dimensional real-world data more efficiently. Although these models have numerous applications, they also have a fundamental limitation of requiring extensive real-world data to function optimally. In the field of robotics, gathering sufficient real-world data can be both impractical and costly. In light of this challenge, we present an innovative solution that leverages the potential of pre-training generative models on large-scale datasets, thereby reducing the amount of data required for data-hungry models to perform optimally.

This research introduces a data compression method rooted in machine learning, specifically the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), which excels in handling noisy data. The algorithm comprises a set of convolutional layers, an autoencoder that adapts to changing data, and a loss function that incorporates noise reduction. Its performance is demonstrated through experiments on MNIST and CelebA datasets, outperforming existing data compression methods and Zip in various metrics, including visual quality, storage efficiency, and noise reduction capabilities.

Analyzing the thermodynamic behavior of the Large Magellanic Cloud's interstellar medium, researchers have identified distinct phases of matter. These phases are separated by phase transitions exhibiting unique thermodynamic properties. To understand these phases, a simplified model of the ILCM's interstellar medium is developed. This model reduces complex equations to equations describing a system of two non-interacting point particles in an external potential, which are derived from equations of magnetohydrodynamics. These reductions retain essential features of the original system, allowing for the identification of phase transitions and regions corresponding to different states of matter. These transitions occur at specific temperatures and depend on the masses of the particles involved.

This research investigates low-energy particle production through the interaction of 4He ions with light targets, specifically 6Li, 7Li, 9Be, 12C, 14N, 16O, 19F, 27Al, 40Ca, 64Ni, and 208Pb. Additionally, data for 208Pb was not included in the initial publication due to an error. Cross-sectional measurements for 4He interactions were compared to those for 2H, with findings showing 4He cross-sections exceeding deuteron cross-sections at lower energies, but the ratio decreasing at higher energies. Further analysis revealed that 4He direct capture cross-sections for all targets exceeded those for deuteron direct capture. Cross-section data for 4He were found to be in line with theoretical predictions from the semi-classical model of Sauter, with some exceptions for 64Ni and 208Pb which exhibited reduced cross-sections likely due to target saturation.

The Pacific Lamprey, a species of jawless fish, has the unique ability to climb smooth surfaces by generating stable undulating waves on their bodies, allowing them to move forward at a speed of up to 1.5 cm per second. Inspired by this capability, our team has developed a robot named Trident, which, like the Pacific Lamprey, uses body undulations to navigate its environment. By integrating this motion with the use of sensors and the ability to adjust their wave patterns, both the fish and our robot have discovered a successful strategy for climbing. Our team's initial tests show that our robot can climb at speeds comparable to the Pacific Lamprey, and with additional development, it could be used to create a successful lamprey replica that surpasses the fish's climbing potential.

This study examines the effects of Doxorubicin and IL-2 therapy on a colon cancer model, utilizing data-driven modeling and advanced mathematical analysis. Doxorubicin's adverse effects on cancer cells' survival and drug resistance are countered by its impact on healthy cells, whereas IL-2 promotes the growth of T-cells but is suppressed by soluble receptors. By incorporating Doxorubicin's dosing schedules and a mathematical model of the IL-2 dosing strategy, we simulate the co-treatment's influence on the cancer microenvironment and the immune system's response. Our results, obtained from applying metropolis-hastings sampling and a terrain-mapping method, indicate that Doxorubicin and IL-2 co-treatment can enhance the immune system's response to colon cancer, enabling the system to traverse the "valley of death" and achieve long-term remission.

This study explores the relationship between maximizing communication system throughput and minimizing the age of information (AoI). We demonstrate that prioritizing throughput in wireless communications can lead to increased AoI, and the extent of this increase depends on the channel's coherence time. To minimize AoI while maintaining high throughput, we propose a new approach that balances these objectives by using a single update at intervals, and analyze the resulting performance.

Research by Chae and Huh (2021) demonstrated that helicity is conserved for certain weak solutions to the 3D Euler equations, specifically in the space $L^\infty_t L^2_x$. This work extends that finding, proving helicity conservation for the 3D Euler equations, as well as a broader class of active scalar equations, including the Euler equations and 2D Burgers equations, without relying on time integration.

Assessments of asymptotic behavior in geometrical optics are made using a specific potential with limited reach, centered directly on the origin. We refine these assessments with more precise mathematical equations.

We've developed an analytical model for the evolution of eccentricities in compact binary systems, valid for any degree of orbital hardening and up to second-order effects in the evolution parameter. Our findings indicate that, under certain conditions, the eccentricity at detection by gravitational-wave interferometers is significantly higher than previously thought. To illustrate this, we've created easy-to-use tables and an online tool to predict the final eccentricities corresponding to specific masses and initial conditions.

A new type of high-intensity, low-repetition-rate X-ray light source is being developed using a planar free-electron laser design. By incorporating an advanced seeding system and a modified undulator design, the research team has achieved a significant breakthrough. They have successfully produced extremely bright X-ray pulses, with a peak intensity of around 10^15 W/um^2, and a high peak power of about 10^17 Watts. This can be compared to the current state-of-the-art facilities, which typically produce less intense X-ray pulses due to their size limitations. The new design also offers a high degree of stability and a short pulse duration of around 100 picoseconds, making it ideal for various groundbreaking experiments.

Recent advances in graph neural networks have led to significant breakthroughs in various graph-related tasks. However, handling complex and evolving graphs remains a persistent challenge. Existing methods for event detection in graphs have limitations in addressing these issues. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a novel approach called DyGED, which effectively integrates entity embeddings, edge predictions, and entity creation in dynamic graphs. By introducing dynamic entity embeddings, our framework adapts to graph changes and maintains consistency across the graph temporally. Additionally, we develop a graph structure evolution module that enables dynamic graph generation and edge prediction. Through our dyEDGCN model, which combines dynamic graph generation and event detection, we demonstrate that DyGED outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for event detection in graphs.

A common method for validating hydrodynamic codes involves comparing their numerical solutions to the well-documented Guderley problem analytical solutions on self-similar implosion. Although many groups utilize hydrodynamic codes to study the complex plasma interactions within inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments, an issue arises as the hydrodynamic and kinetic approaches diverge in their treatment of kinetic plasma effects. To address this discrepancy, we have developed an extended version of the Guderley problem that accounts for the kinetic approach, including the distribution of particle velocities and the resulting nonequilibrium plasma conditions. Our analytical model incorporates the effects of reduced distribution functions and does not rely on the traditional Maxwellian distribution, thereby enabling the comparison of analytical and numerical solutions for self-consistent inertial confinement fusion simulations.

Although requirements engineering plays a crucial role in the development of software systems, its potential benefits in creating more transparent and understandable AI (explainable AI) are often overlooked. In this context, we are interested in the characteristics of data, data sources, and how humans interact with AI that make it user-friendly. In our research, we aim to understand how requirements engineering can lead to the development of more understandable AI systems by involving various stakeholders throughout the process. By doing so, we can ensure that the created AI systems are designed to be easily comprehensible to users, thus promoting their adoption and effectiveness.

Colorectal adenomas are the primary precursor to colorectal cancer, and their identification during colonoscopy is crucial for effective treatment. Although colonoscopy allows for direct visualization, determining the presence and severity of adenomas relies on the expertise of gastroenterologists who interpret the images. To improve this process, a novel technique combining deep neural networks and image analysis was developed to assess and categorize colorectal adenomas based on specific visual features. By analyzing the components of the images, such as polyp morphology and vascular patterns, this method can identify and classify adenomas more accurately. When tested on a dataset of simulated colonoscopy images, the technique demonstrated its potential for aiding gastroenterologists in categorizing and identifying adenomas more effectively.

A novel mathematical framework is introduced to analyze fixed-length source coding schemes, focusing on the interplay between optimal normalized leakage and optimal compression rates. We examine a specific scenario in which compression is optimized while a certain amount of data leakage is allowed, revealing a linear relationship between normalized leakage and optimal compression rate for small values of leakage, for various types of source distributions. We also explore this proportional leakage coding concept in two specific source distribution cases: uniform distributions and geometric distributions, for which we explicitly calculate the optimal compression rates. Additionally, we extend our analysis to distributed source coding by examining a specific scenario in which encoders are optimized while allowing a certain amount of data leakage, revealing a proportional leakage coding region for distributions that are either uniform or have monotone distributions.

We introduce MrSARP, an image-synthesizing system that generates multi-scale images aligned with real-world data, capable of producing images at various resolutions in a single step. For lower-resolution images, MrSARP demonstrates equal performance to state-of-the-art models, while outperforming them at higher resolutions. Additionally, MrSARP exhibits improved likelihood scores, lower compression artifacts, and higher perceptual quality according to both automated and human evaluations. The model's parameters can also be efficiently transferred to other models to enhance their likelihood scores and compression quality.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) has been proposed as a potential approach to tackle complex combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, due to the complex process of adjusting its adjustable settings, QAOA has a high barrier to overcoming the "barren plateau" issue. In this research, we integrate Bayesian optimization with QAOA for solving the 0/1 knapsack problem, and our findings show that hybrid QAOA-BO outperforms hybrid QAOA alone and other classical methods in terms of solution quality and computational time, and we hope that this research will provide valuable insights for developing more effective hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in the future.
We've developed an algorithm to identify the intersection points of two ellipses by directly solving their equations, and another variant that determines if circular quads intersect at all.

Actor-Critic algorithms, a class of reinforcement learning methods, address
the challenge of estimating action-value functions, often referred to as the Q-function.
Many existing actor-critic algorithms, such as those based on policy gradient,
address the resulting density function of the Q-function's Gibbs measure in an
inefficient manner, leading to a common issue of mode hunting. In our approach,
we address this limitation by introducing a new estimation technique for the
variance, utilizing a Bayesian estimator that incorporates information about
the Q-function. Building on this concept, we propose a new algorithm, referred to
as the Variance-estimating Actor-Critic (VAC), which integrates this
estimation technique and demonstrates improved performance, particularly
resulting in lower sample complexity and faster convergence rates, according to
our theoretical analysis. Our results, validated through experiments on grid-world
environments, show that VAC achieves superior performance compared to existing
Actor-Critic algorithms, including those based on policy gradient.

A study of stripe order in the Hubbard and related models reveals that quantum fluctuations are crucial for stabilizing this order, particularly near phase boundaries where thermal fluctuations are insufficient. Our analysis employs a dynamic mean-field theory that accounts for fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation through corrections derived from Gaussian fluctuations. These corrections are significant and positively influence stripe stability, particularly in thermal conditions. Furthermore, strain-induced stripe transitions are investigated, demonstrating that boundary effects can result in an emergence of a stable stripe phase that exceeds typical system-size limitations.

Automatically locating individual vertebrae within CT scans is crucial for medical research and diagnosis. However, current methods for this task have limitations in accuracy and usability. To address these issues, we've developed a new approach combining weakly-supervised learning and morphological analysis. This method marks the beginning of each vertebrae using only spinal section images and their corresponding CT scans. By leveraging 3D CT scans, we can generate precise markers at specific depths along the spine's surface to identify the bone's exact location. Our experiments demonstrate that this method achieves superior accuracy compared to the current best technique, with a 10% improvement and nearly perfect recall rates. Additionally, it processes and labels a single vertebral segment in just 0.03 seconds, showcasing its exceptional computational efficiency.

The study of Markovian spin systems, consisting of a large number of coupled spins, leverages the algebraic and topological framework of Markovian models to streamline the computation of asymptotic averages and correlation integrals. These frameworks are inherently discrete and thus facilitate the analysis of the systems' collective dynamics. However, this approach is limited to the calculation of correlation integrals up to a certain order $2n$, where $n$ represents the number of spins. A key aspect of this limitation lies in the requirement for the Hamiltonian to be expressed as a polynomial of degree $2n$ in creation and annihilation operators. Consequently, this formalism is not applicable to all types of physical interactions, such as the dipolar interaction, which do not conform to this operator structure. To address this shortcoming, an alternative approach is proposed, involving a modified Hamiltonian that is equivalent to the original up to correction terms. These terms, although generally complex, can be simplified under specific conditions, thereby extending the applicability of the correlation integral calculation to higher orders.

We have computed the Hodge--Zeta function for toric complete intersections with smooth additional divisors, and as a result, we can derive the relative zeta functions among the I-functions, and between the I-functions and the L-functions, and also find the relative L-functions among the zeta functions.

This study develops a piezoelectric complete transmission condition, which can be effectively used to eliminate traces in an acoustic scattering problem with obstacles of complex shapes. The condition is found to be equivalent to a surface integral condition derived from the fundamental solution of the piezoelectric equation. The implementation of the condition leads to a integral equation that must be solved to find the solution. The stability of the implementation is confirmed through estimates of the associated operator on specific function spaces, which in turn establish the stability of the scattering problem. Additionally, we prove the stability of the implementation in the high-frequency regime.

A key aspect of manipulating polariton condensates in optical systems involves the spatial manipulation of the excitation beam, which in turn affects the photon wavefunction and coupling to the matter component. This research focuses on an optical setup designed to create intricate patterns of ground-state amplitude distributions and explores the resulting impact on radial polariton condensates. By combining these patterns with repulsive potential barriers, stable radial condensates can be formed and their properties, such as coherence and phase structure, can be manipulated. Additionally, a new class of polariton laser that operates in multiple spatial modes and produces coherent ring patterns has been demonstrated experimentally.

The exoplanet K2-22 b, which orbits very close to its host star, is thought to be a mini-Neptune with an estimated size of about 1.5 times that of Earth. Due to its proximity, it is likely losing its atmosphere at a high rate, which could result in the complete loss of the planet within a relatively short astronomical timeframe of about 10 million years. Recent observations using the High Resolution Spectrograph on the Large Binocular Telescope have provided the first measurements of the atmosphere of K2-22 b. These measurements indicate that the atmosphere is present and is likely located at a relatively low altitude, which is about 1000 kilometers above the planet's surface. This low altitude is attributed to the high temperature of the atmosphere, which is about 2000 Kelvin, as well as the low mass of the planet, which is about 5.5 times that of Earth. These measurements are consistent with the predictions of the models of the atmosphere of K2-22 b, which suggest that the atmosphere is present and is likely located at a relatively low altitude, which is about 1000 kilometers above the planet's surface.

We are investigating the classification of irreducible binary forms up to classification by diffeomorphism of their associated Milnor fibration. Initially, Broughton's work demonstrates that such a classification results in a finite number of distinct classes. Subsequently, building on D\'uval's theorem, we show that each class contains only a finite number of binary forms with a specified degree.

This research introduces FastPy, an interpreter written in C#, which translates and runs Python code. The study focuses on implementing an intermediate representation in C# that can be utilized by both C# and Python libraries, particularly those working with numerical data in multi-dimensional arrays. C#'s similar library to Python's NumPy, called Span, forms the basis of FastPy's intermediate representation.

In the 17th century, scientists like Galileo adopted the term 'principle' to describe fundamental aspects of nature that couldn't be fully explained through experimentation alone. However, nature's basic workings were considered too complex to be comprehensively explored empirically. Given this limitation, scientists focused on establishing the basic aspects of nature through experimentation, using the phrase 'to principle' to describe contributing significantly to understanding those fundamental workings. Despite his notable discoveries, Galileo's inability to fully explain nature's basic workings meant he wasn't seen as making a substantial impact on understanding nature's basic workings.

A generalised form of binding q-energy is developed, which is suitable for systems governed by non-Gaussian distributions characterized by a specific q-value. This q-binding energy can be seen as a broader version of traditional binding energy, which is applicable to systems with Gaussian distributions. The q-binding energy is particularly useful for systems exhibiting power-law distributions, for which a specific formula can be used to calculate its value. The principles of both q-binding energy and q-entropy are seen as fundamental laws, which can be used to derive additional system properties, such as the average fractional binding q-energy. This is similar to the principles of traditional energy, which can give rise to concepts like the Gibbs fractional energy.

In a magnetic island coalescence scenario, we examine the interaction between magnetohydrodynamic scales and the electron cyclotron frequency within a resistive slab. By applying a semi- analytical method, we develop models for island width evolution, reconnection rate, and the distribution of electron and ion temperatures, which are influenced by magnetic fluctuations. Our results reveal that ion temperature anisotropy can trigger the electron cyclotron mode, leading to parallel electron cooling and a sudden decrease in the island's reconnection rate.

To effectively work with humans, autonomous systems must adapt their behavior based on the specific task at hand and any existing partnerships they have. Adaptive digital assistants need to develop long-term strategies and a basic understanding of their partners, which requires persistent learning across various applications and environments. We propose a new framework that enables these assistants to learn and evolve over time, working within a collaborative setting where human-DA pairs work together on a range of collaborative tasks. Within this framework, we introduce a network for memory, which helps these assistants retain and apply knowledge from past collaborations, and a system for managing their memories, which decides when to store new experiences and makes them applicable to new situations. We demonstrate the benefits of this framework through a series of collaborative tasks, showing how this approach can improve their performance and adapt to different partnerships and tasks.
